punctuated: 甞以之自恃哉？故人知其治化之成於天下者，有雍和熈皥之盛，而不知其本原之地、隱微之中，固有曰嚴曰愼，而非人之所能窺者。是故曰兢兢，曰業業，曰祗台，曰昭格，曰緝熈執競，此其持敬之心，所以畏天者不敢怠也。曰允執厥中，曰惟精惟一，曰不自滿假，曰日新又新，曰望道未見，敬義交修，此其務實之學，所以憲天者不容已也。夫既有神聖之資，而存之以無敢暇豫之心，濟之以惟日不足之學，則德業之盛，固已各臻其極，而當時輔理成化之臣，宜無有能增益之者。然皐陶之謨、益稷之戒、伊尹之訓、周召之誥，每惓惓焉，蓋不因其君之已聖，而遂忘其獻納之忠；而爲之君者，亦不自以爲聖，而遂忽於聽受之益。此其君臣交相儆戒，而均之以畏天爲心；上下互相資益，而均之以憲天爲學。唐虞三代之治，所以臻於隆盛之極，而數聖人者
translation_en:
…ever relied complacently upon it? Thus people know that the transforming influence of their government brought magnificent harmony and radiant concord throughout the realm. Yet they do not know that, at its source, within the hidden recesses of their hearts, lay a solemnity and caution beyond others’ ability to discern. Hence the expressions “watchful,” “vigilant,” “I am reverent,” “illustriously reaching [Heaven],” and “continuing in brightness and holding firmly to strength.” These describe their reverent disposition: in fearing Heaven, they dared not relax. The expressions “sincerely hold fast to the mean,” “be discerning and single-minded,” “do not deem yourself fully accomplished,” “renew yourself daily, and renew yourself yet again,” and “look toward the Way as though you had not yet seen it” describe the joint cultivation of reverence and righteousness. Such was their learning directed toward real practice: in modeling themselves upon Heaven, they could not cease.

Possessing the endowments of divine sages, they preserved them with hearts that dared not indulge in leisure or pleasure, and supplemented them with learning for which the days never seemed sufficient. The fullness of their virtue and achievement had thus already reached its utmost limit in each case, and it might seem that the ministers who assisted their rule and brought its transforming work to completion could have added nothing further. Yet the counsels of Gao Yao, the admonitions of Yi and Ji, the instructions of Yi Yin, and the announcements of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao were continually earnest. These ministers did not forget their loyal duty to offer counsel merely because their rulers were already sages; nor did their rulers, regarding themselves as sages, neglect the benefits of listening to and accepting advice. Thus rulers and ministers admonished and warned one another, sharing a disposition of awe toward Heaven; superiors and subordinates helped and strengthened one another, sharing a commitment to learning that took Heaven as its model. This is why the government of Tang and Yu and of the Three Dynasties reached the utmost height of flourishing achievement, and why those several sages…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
固若乎曠世而相感也漢唐以來英誼間
出雖未可以神聖言而亦天之所厚寄以
君師之責者然不能體天之心而持敬務
學以濟其所不及則其所就之卑也固宜
自今觀之牢祀孔子若知所宗矣而不事
詩書雖陸生無以挽其習詔置博士若有
所興矣而未遑禮樂雖賈誼無以正其趨
表章六經者志非不銳也卒馳於窮兵而
輪臺之誨莫追召集名儒者講非不勤也
===
卒昵於恭顯而甘露之危途釀親幸大學
徒高息馬論道之風駕臨辟雍未究執經
問難之實考定五經者宜其有稽古之益
也其如貞觀之治大綱未正何更日侍讀
者宜其有納約之功也其如開元之政鮮
克有終何有宋諸君多稱好學然務博覽
而義理未明工書翰而身心無補賢如二
程而不見知學如朱子而不見用類皆外
侈美觀之具內無敬學之心卽其侍從諸
punctuated: 固若乎曠世而相感也。漢唐以來，英誼間出，雖未可以神聖言，而亦天之所厚寄以君師之責者。然不能體天之心，而持敬務學以濟其所不及，則其所就之卑也固宜。自今觀之，牢祀孔子，若知所宗矣，而不事詩書，雖陸生無以挽其習；詔置博士，若有所興矣，而未遑禮樂，雖賈誼無以正其趨。表章六經者，志非不銳也，卒馳於窮兵，而輪臺之誨莫追；召集名儒者，講非不勤也，卒昵於恭顯，而甘露之危途釀。親幸大學，徒高息馬論道之風；駕臨辟雍，未究執經問難之實。考定五經者，宜其有稽古之益也，其如貞觀之治大綱未正何？更日侍讀者，宜其有納約之功也，其如開元之政鮮克有終何？有宋諸君，多稱好學，然務博覽而義理未明，工書翰而身心無補。賢如二程而不見知，學如朱子而不見用，類皆外侈美觀之具，內無敬學之心。卽其侍從諸
translation_en:
…indeed seemed to respond to one another across the ages. From the Han and Tang onward, rulers of outstanding ability and righteousness [?] appeared from time to time. Though they could not yet be called divine sages, they were nevertheless men to whom Heaven had entrusted the weighty responsibilities of ruler and teacher. Yet they could not embody Heaven’s mind, maintain reverence, and devote themselves to learning in order to remedy their shortcomings. It was therefore only to be expected that their achievements would be modest.

Viewed from the present, offering an animal sacrifice to Confucius seemed to show an understanding of whom to revere; yet the ruler did not apply himself to the Odes and Documents, and even Master Lu could not turn him from his accustomed ways. Ordering the establishment of Erudites seemed to promise a revival of learning; yet the ruler found no time for rites and music, and even Jia Yi could not correct his course. The ruler who exalted the Six Classics certainly did not lack resolve, but ultimately pursued military campaigns to exhaustion, and the admonition issued at Luntai could not undo what had happened. The ruler who assembled eminent Confucian scholars certainly did not lack diligence in scholarly discussion, but ultimately grew attached to Gong and Xian, thereby setting a dangerous course during the Ganlu era [?]. A personal visit to the Imperial University merely exalted the example of resting the warhorses and discussing the Way; an imperial visit to the Biyong did not fully realize the substance of taking up the Classics and questioning difficult passages.

The ruler who had the Five Classics examined and established should have benefited from investigating antiquity; yet what can be said of the failure to rectify the fundamental principles of government during the Zhenguan era? The ruler who had lecturers attend him on alternate days should have benefited from their concise counsel; yet what can be said of the failure to bring the government of the Kaiyuan era to a good conclusion?

The rulers of the Song were often praised for their love of learning. Yet they pursued extensive reading without clarifying moral principles, and excelled in calligraphy and composition without benefiting their own persons and minds. Men as worthy as the two Cheng brothers went unrecognized, and one as learned as Master Zhu went unused. In general, these rulers lavishly displayed the outward trappings of learning, while inwardly lacking a reverent commitment to it. As for their various attendant…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
臣或俳優而不根或靡麗而無當既不足
以稱啓沃至於正言弼直經學淵源之士
則又厭而不聽甚者斥而遠之所謂聽古
樂惟恐臥聞新聲即不知倦也欲論思之
有益而聖學之復明也得乎此所以雜霸
雜夷仁柔不振而其治去唐虞三代遠甚
矣天啓我
高皇帝應運而作得國之正本與帝王同符敬
學之傳又於精一默契初輯干戈即遣祭
===
於闕里初置郡邑即申誥乎學規操存之
要無暇逸則於學士宋濂發之堯舜之治
皆由中則於侍郎曾魯發之存心有錄見
人君以天之心爲心也而欽若之道以崇
省躬有錄見人臣以君之心爲心也而交
儆之誠益至疏尚書洪範於座右其揖箕
子於神交乎書大學衍義於兩廡其臣德
秀於異代乎雖
聖衷之蘊廣遠難窺而敷言具存焯爍可頌二
punctuated:
臣，或俳優而不根，或靡麗而無當，既不足以稱啓沃；至於正言弼直、經學淵源之士，則又厭而不聽，甚者斥而遠之。所謂聽古樂惟恐臥，聞新聲即不知倦也。欲論思之有益，而聖學之復明也，得乎？此所以雜霸雜夷，仁柔不振，而其治去唐虞三代遠甚矣。
天啓我高皇帝，應運而作，得國之正，本與帝王同符；敬學之傳，又於精一默契。初輯干戈，即遣祭於闕里；初置郡邑，即申誥乎學規。操存之要，無暇逸，則於學士宋濂發之；堯舜之治，皆由中，則於侍郎曾魯發之。存心有錄，見人君以天之心爲心也，而欽若之道以崇；省躬有錄，見人臣以君之心爲心也，而交儆之誠益至。疏《尚書》《洪範》於座右，其揖箕子於神交乎？書《大學衍義》於兩廡，其臣德秀於異代乎？雖聖衷之蘊，廣遠難窺，而敷言具存，焯爍可頌。二
translation_en:
…ministers attending them were either buffoonish and without foundation, or florid and without substance, and thus unworthy of being credited with enlightening and nourishing their rulers’ minds. As for men whose upright words offered forthright correction and whose classical learning had deep roots, the rulers wearied of them and would not listen; worse still, they dismissed them and sent them far away. This is what is meant by fearing one will fall asleep when hearing ancient music, yet never tiring of new tunes. Could one hope that deliberation and reflection would prove beneficial and that sagely learning would shine forth again? This is why their government mingled hegemonic practices with barbarian ways, while their benevolence was weak and ineffectual, and why their rule fell so far short of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties.
Heaven guided our Emperor Gao, who arose in response to the appointed destiny. The legitimacy of his acquisition of the realm accorded with that of the ancient emperors and kings; in transmitting reverence for learning, he also tacitly accorded with their teaching of refinement and single-mindedness. As soon as he had stilled the weapons of war, he dispatched an envoy to offer sacrifice at Queli. As soon as he established prefectures and counties, he issued renewed instructions on school regulations. He explained to Academician Song Lian that the essential requirement for holding fast to and preserving the mind was to allow no idle ease; he explained to Vice Minister Zeng Lu that the government of Yao and Shun arose entirely from within. His record on preserving the mind shows that a ruler takes Heaven’s mind as his own, thereby exalting the way of reverent conformity to Heaven. His record on examining oneself shows that a minister takes his ruler’s mind as his own, thereby deepening the sincerity of mutual admonition. By setting out the “Great Plan” chapter of the Book of Documents beside his seat, was he not saluting Jizi in spiritual communion? By having the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning inscribed in the two side galleries, was he not taking Zhen Dexiu as his minister across the ages? Although the riches within his sagely heart were too vast and far-reaching to fathom, his pronouncements survive in full, shining brilliantly and deserving praise. The Two…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
帝三王此振其緒
聖子神孫此培其基矣在
文皇帝得之而敦崇道術故不惟表章經書以
廣聖賢傳心之典而又闡著心法以揭帝
王創守之規在
章皇帝得之而雅懋聖脩故不但編緝倫書秩
秩乎嘉言善行之具載而又
親製帝訓懍懍乎父作子述之維艱至若增籩
豆舞佾之儀於孔廟者我
===
純皇帝也心旣切於崇儒訓獨先於務學乃猶
日就經筵時歷寒暑而不輟則所以涵養
此心者無寧時矣廣校宫横舍之制於闕
里者我
敬皇帝也志旣殷於慕聖禮不靳於尊師乃猶
虚受箴規語涉危亡而不忌則所以緝熈
此學者無逸志矣此皆學術之大後先一
揆者暨我
□宗肅皇帝則益闡揚而光大之朝御
punctuated: 帝三王，此振其緒；聖子神孫，此培其基矣。在文皇帝得之，而敦崇道術，故不惟表章經書，以廣聖賢傳心之典，而又闡著心法，以揭帝王創守之規。在章皇帝得之，而雅懋聖脩，故不但編緝倫書，秩秩乎嘉言善行之具載，而又親製帝訓，懍懍乎父作子述之維艱。至若增籩豆舞佾之儀於孔廟者，我純皇帝也。心旣切於崇儒，訓獨先於務學，乃猶日就經筵，時歷寒暑而不輟，則所以涵養此心者，無寧時矣。廣校宫横舍之制於闕里者，我敬皇帝也。志旣殷於慕聖，禮不靳於尊師，乃猶虚受箴規，語涉危亡而不忌，則所以緝熈此學者，無逸志矣。此皆學術之大，後先一揆者。暨我□宗肅皇帝，則益闡揚而光大之，朝御
translation_en:
…the [Two] Emperors and Three Kings: through this their legacy was carried forward; sagely sons and divine grandsons: through this their foundation was strengthened. Emperor Wen grasped this and earnestly honored the Way and its learning. Thus he not only gave prominence to the Confucian classics, expanding the canon through which sages and worthies transmitted their understanding of the mind, but also elucidated the methods of cultivating the mind, setting forth the rules by which emperors and kings found and preserve their realms. Emperor Zhang grasped this and assiduously pursued sagely self-cultivation. Thus he not only compiled writings on human relationships, systematically recording exemplary words and good deeds in full, but also personally composed the Imperial Instructions, expressing profound awe at the difficulty of a father’s founding work and a son’s continuation of it.

As for the emperor who augmented the rites governing bamboo and wooden offering vessels and the ranks of dancers at the temple of Confucius, this was our Emperor Chun. His concern for honoring Confucian learning was already ardent, and his instructions gave foremost place to diligent study. Yet he still attended the Classics Colloquium daily, continuing through cold and heat without interruption. Thus he never rested in nurturing this mind. The emperor who expanded the provision of school buildings and study quarters [?] at Queli was our Emperor Jing. His resolve to emulate the Sage was already profound, and he spared nothing in the ceremonial honors he accorded teachers. Yet he still humbly accepted admonitions, taking no offense even when they spoke of peril and ruin. Thus he never entertained a wish for ease in bringing this learning to greater brilliance. All these were great achievements in learning, guided by the same standard from one reign to the next. When it came to our Emperor □zong Su, he further expounded and magnified it. In the mornings he attended …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
經筵集思廣益退臨
書幄寡欲清心敬一之旨發千聖未發之心
源箴解之文明諸儒未明之道體以此
敬天法祖以此恭巳臨民攬獨斷之權而六服
羣辟罔不共其令鑒先世之弊而中官外
戚無所售其私是蓋道根於心心一於敬
所以享國長久天下乂安有由然哉今我
皇上當作君作師之初隆善繼善述之道文命
所被薄海嚮風於時肇舉
===
經筵以資輔理
親臨太學以導敬敷
便殿之鼓載鳴而垂紳進講者玉立成均之
蹕甫駐而擊磬雅歌者雲從道闡圖書兆龜
龍之復出光生俎豆將麟鳳以來儀是誠
躬帝王之資而興唐虞三代之學者也謂
尚不足以風天下乎昔者辟雍創於鎬京
而周詠思服泮宮環於璧水而魯頌采芹
愚生竊在菁莪樂育之中敢自後於橋門
punctuated:
經筵，集思廣益；退臨書幄，寡欲清心。《敬一》之旨，發千聖未發之心源；《箴解》之文，明諸儒未明之道體。以此敬天法祖，以此恭巳臨民。攬獨斷之權，而六服羣辟罔不共其令；鑒先世之弊，而中官外戚無所售其私。是蓋道根於心，心一於敬，所以享國長久、天下乂安，有由然哉！
今我皇上當作君作師之初，隆善繼善述之道，文命所被，薄海嚮風。於時肇舉經筵，以資輔理；親臨太學，以導敬敷。便殿之鼓載鳴，而垂紳進講者玉立；成均之蹕甫駐，而擊磬雅歌者雲從。道闡圖書，兆龜龍之復出；光生俎豆，將麟鳳以來儀。是誠躬帝王之資，而興唐虞三代之學者也。謂尚不足以風天下乎？
昔者辟雍創於鎬京，而周詠思服；泮宮環於璧水，而魯頌采芹。愚生竊在菁莪樂育之中，敢自後於橋門
translation_en:
…at the Classics Colloquium, he pooled counsel and drew widely upon its benefits; withdrawing to his study, he restrained his desires and purified his mind. The purport of Reverence for the One (Jingyi) disclosed the wellspring of the mind that a thousand sages had not disclosed; the text of Explanations of the Admonitions (Zhenjie) clarified the substance of the Way that the Confucian scholars had not clarified. Through this he revered Heaven and took his ancestors as models; through this he disciplined himself reverently and governed the people. He held the power of sole decision, and none of the rulers throughout the six zones of allegiance failed to obey his commands. Taking warning from the abuses of earlier reigns, he left palace eunuchs and imperial relatives by marriage no opportunity to advance their private interests. Here indeed the Way was rooted in the mind, and the mind was unified in reverence. Surely there were grounds for his long reign and the peace and good order of the realm!
Now, at the outset of his service as ruler and teacher, our present Emperor exalts the Way of worthily continuing and carrying forward his predecessor’s work. Wherever his civilizing commands reach, to the very borders of the seas, all turn toward his influence. He has accordingly inaugurated the Classics Colloquium to assist his governance and personally visited the Imperial University to lead the reverent dissemination of instruction. As the drum sounds in the side hall, those presenting lectures stand upright like jade, their ceremonial sashes hanging down. No sooner has the imperial procession halted at the university than those striking musical stones and singing refined songs gather like clouds. The Way is elucidated in the River Chart and Luo Writing, presaging the renewed appearance of the numinous tortoise and dragon; radiance shines upon the sacrificial vessels, about to draw the qilin and phoenix to appear in auspicious majesty. Truly, he embodies the endowments of emperors and kings and revives the learning of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Could one say that this is still insufficient to transform the realm through his example?
In former times, when the royal academy was founded at Haojing, the Zhou ode sang of devoted reflection; when the Pan Palace stood encircled by its jade-disc waters, the Lu hymn celebrated gathering water celery. I, an unworthy student, have been fortunate enough to receive the joyful nurture celebrated in the ode Luxuriant Southernwood. How could I dare lag behind those at the academy’s bridge gate…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
圜聽之列但稽首揚厲莫罄名言至欲有
補論思槩乎莫知所以雖然竊聞之矣九
九之術敢於賓齊食芹而甘者不知有玉
食而思獻况明問及之敢不攄其一得之
愚哉是故責實者不徇其名美成者在端
其始然則有唐虞三代之舉動矣而猶未
覩其實功有唐虞三代之造端矣而尚未
臻其成效君子能無慮乎姑即今日
皇上之學言之
===
經筵之御崇儒之心也將
經筵之一御而謂足以盡崇儒之實也可乎
大學之臨重道之心也將大學之一臨而
謂足以盡重道之實也可乎故方其
御講之時蓋聞乎聖人之言矣義理之感發必
有勃然而聽之忘倦者吾不知退而優游
泮渙之時猶能尋而繹之以求其精義之
歸乎抑師保之不臨而惟其心之所好以
馳騖於他技已也方其
punctuated:
圜聽之列，但稽首揚厲，莫罄名言。至欲有補論思，槩乎莫知所以。雖然，竊聞之矣：九九之術，敢於賓齊；食芹而甘者，不知有玉食而思獻。况明問及之，敢不攄其一得之愚哉？是故責實者不徇其名，美成者在端其始。然則有唐虞三代之舉動矣，而猶未覩其實功；有唐虞三代之造端矣，而尚未臻其成效，君子能無慮乎？姑即今日皇上之學言之。
經筵之御，崇儒之心也。將經筵之一御，而謂足以盡崇儒之實也，可乎？大學之臨，重道之心也。將大學之一臨，而謂足以盡重道之實也，可乎？故方其御講之時，蓋聞乎聖人之言矣，義理之感發，必有勃然而聽之忘倦者。吾不知退而優游泮渙之時，猶能尋而繹之，以求其精義之歸乎？抑師保之不臨，而惟其心之所好，以馳騖於他技已也？方其
translation_en:
…the ranks of those gathered round to listen. I can only bow my head and proclaim these glories, which words cannot fully express. As for contributing to deliberation and reflection, I scarcely know how. Yet I have heard that a man with only the multiplication table to offer dared seek reception as a guest in Qi; and that someone who found celery sweet, unaware of exquisite delicacies, wished to present it to his ruler. Since your discerning question has reached even this matter, dare I fail to express the one small insight of my foolish understanding? Thus, those who demand substance do not pursue mere names, and a fine accomplishment depends on setting its beginnings right. If there are actions like those of the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, yet their substantial achievements remain unseen; if there are beginnings like theirs, yet their full results remain unrealized—can a gentleman be free of concern? Let us speak, then, of His Majesty’s learning today.
His attendance at the Classics Colloquium expresses his intention to honor Confucian scholars. But can a single attendance be deemed sufficient to fulfill that intention in substance? His visit to the Imperial University expresses his intention to esteem the Way. But can a single visit be deemed sufficient to fulfill that intention in substance? When he attends the lectures, he hears the words of the sages. Stirred by their moral principles, he must surely experience moments of sudden inspiration, listening without weariness. I do not know whether, after withdrawing into leisure and relaxation, he can still examine and ponder them, seeking the ultimate import of their profound principles. Or, when his preceptors and guardians are absent, does he simply follow his own inclinations and pursue other skills? When he…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
幸學之際蓋游於聖人之門矣道德之儀刑必
有奮然而從之末由者吾不知退而燕居
獨處之際猶能常目在之以永其寤寐之
思乎抑宮牆之旣遠而惟其身之所接以
依違乎近習已也夫一暴十寒非所以進
於善也理欲交戰非所以純其心也况荒
寧是懼則二帝三王之成憲具昭存省有
常則
二祖列聖之家敎如在是故始之以務學之勤
===
而遜志時敏則寒暑不輟如
憲皇可也廣之以虛受之益而樂善兼容則箴
規不忘如
孝皇可也由是而存心以端其本則幾微必審
也由是而省躬以防其欲則舉動必愼也
經書之表章者不惟玩其議論而深思其
心法之精倫書之編輯者不惟考其典故
而力求其身體之實是故他技雖足以投
吾好也而此心常若保傅之在前近習雖
punctuated: 幸學之際，蓋游於聖人之門矣。道德之儀刑，必有奮然而從之末由者。吾不知退而燕居獨處之際，猶能常目在之，以永其寤寐之思乎？抑宮牆之旣遠，而惟其身之所接，以依違乎近習已也？夫一暴十寒，非所以進於善也；理欲交戰，非所以純其心也。况荒寧是懼，則二帝三王之成憲具昭；存省有常，則二祖列聖之家敎如在。是故始之以務學之勤，而遜志時敏，則寒暑不輟，如憲皇可也；廣之以虛受之益，而樂善兼容，則箴規不忘，如孝皇可也。由是而存心，以端其本，則幾微必審也；由是而省躬，以防其欲，則舉動必愼也。經書之表章者，不惟玩其議論，而深思其心法之精；倫書之編輯者，不惟考其典故，而力求其身體之實。是故他技雖足以投吾好也，而此心常若保傅之在前；近習雖
translation_en:
…when you visit the imperial school, you have indeed entered the gate of the sages. Before their exemplary moral virtue, you must surely feel stirred to follow them, yet find no way to do so. I do not know whether, after withdrawing to dwell quietly and alone, you can still keep them constantly before your eyes, sustaining your thoughts of them waking and sleeping. Or, once far from the school’s walls, do you merely accommodate yourself to familiar attendants, guided only by those with whom you personally associate? One day of warmth followed by ten days of cold is no way to advance in goodness; allowing moral principle and desire to contend is no way to make the heart pure. Moreover, if you fear heedless ease, the established models of the Two Emperors and Three Kings stand fully revealed; if you constantly preserve and examine your heart, the family teachings of the two dynastic founders and successive sage emperors remain as though present before you.

Thus, begin with diligence in learning: humble your aspirations and apply yourself assiduously at all times, never ceasing through cold or heat, as Emperor Xian did. Broaden this through the benefits of receptive humility: delight in goodness and embrace others’ strengths, never forgetting admonitions and corrections, as Emperor Xiao did. Through this, preserve your heart to rectify the foundation, and you will surely scrutinize the subtlest stirrings of thought. Through this, examine yourself to guard against desire, and you will surely exercise care in every action. As for the canonical writings you have honored and made prominent, do not merely ponder their discussions, but reflect deeply on the subtleties of their methods for cultivating the heart. As for the writings on human relations [?] you have compiled, do not merely investigate their precedents, but earnestly seek to embody their teachings in practice. Thus, although other pursuits may appeal to my tastes, my heart will always feel as though its guardians and preceptors stood before it; although familiar attendants…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
足以順吾旨也而此心常若聖賢之相對
崇儒而必求真儒則講論切而理可明矣
重道而不惑於非道則趨向一而心可端
矣理明而是非之極自定心端而邪正之
辨自嚴是非之極定於內而凡進言之臣
是者行之非者置之而確乎其不易否則
漫然不加可否雖無拒諫之非而亦未見
有從諫之實也邪正之辨嚴於外而凡效
用之臣正者任之邪者去之而斷乎其無
===
疑否則混然無所決擇雖無遺賢之嘆而
亦未見得任賢之實也嗚呼人君之德存
心務學其大端也君德之用任賢納諫其
大致也從事於四者之間而朝夕匪懈何
患乎德之不盛而業之不廣也哉抑愚生
又有進焉守
祖宗之心法而紹堯舜禹湯文武之傳以無負
於上天付託之意者吾
君之事也廣論思之忠益而繼皐陶伊傅周召
punctuated: 足以順吾旨也，而此心常若聖賢之相對。崇儒而必求真儒，則講論切而理可明矣；重道而不惑於非道，則趨向一而心可端矣。理明而是非之極自定，心端而邪正之辨自嚴。是非之極定於內，而凡進言之臣，是者行之，非者置之，而確乎其不易；否則漫然不加可否，雖無拒諫之非，而亦未見有從諫之實也。邪正之辨嚴於外，而凡效用之臣，正者任之，邪者去之，而斷乎其無疑；否則混然無所決擇，雖無遺賢之嘆，而亦未見得任賢之實也。嗚呼！人君之德，存心務學，其大端也；君德之用，任賢納諫，其大致也。從事於四者之間，而朝夕匪懈，何患乎德之不盛而業之不廣也哉！抑愚生又有進焉：守祖宗之心法，而紹堯舜禹湯文武之傳，以無負於上天付託之意者，吾君之事也；廣論思之忠益，而繼皐陶伊傅周召
translation_en:
…may suffice to comply with my wishes, yet my mind remains as though confronting the sages and worthies. If one honors Confucian scholars and insists on seeking true Confucians, their discussions will be searching, and principle can be made clear. If one esteems the Way and is not misled by what is contrary to it, one’s purposes will be unified, and the mind can be rectified. When principle is clear, the standard of right and wrong naturally becomes settled; when the mind is upright, the distinction between the wicked and the upright naturally becomes strict. With the standard of right and wrong settled within, one puts into practice what is right in the counsel ministers offer and sets aside what is wrong, remaining firm and unwavering. Otherwise, if one heedlessly neither approves nor disapproves, even without the fault of rejecting remonstrance, one has yet to show the substance of heeding it. With the distinction between the wicked and the upright strictly maintained in external affairs, one employs the upright among ministers offering their service and dismisses the wicked, acting decisively and without doubt. Otherwise, if one indiscriminately makes no choice between them, even without complaints that worthy men have been overlooked, one has yet to show the substance of employing them.

Alas! Preserving the moral mind and diligently pursuing learning are the principal elements of a ruler’s virtue; employing worthy men and accepting remonstrance are the principal ways that virtue is put into practice. If one devotes oneself to these four things, never slackening morning or evening, why fear that one’s virtue will not flourish or one’s achievements expand?

Yet I, an ignorant student, have something further to submit. To preserve the ancestral sovereigns’ teachings concerning the mind and continue the tradition of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, thereby fulfilling the intent of Heaven’s charge—this is our ruler’s task. To extend the loyal assistance furnished through deliberation and reflection, and carry forward the accomplishments of Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
之績以無愧於儒者功用之全則諸臣之
責也是故有以玩人喪德玩物喪志敬勝
怠義勝欲之說進者是欲
上爲文武也有以無敎逸欲無曠庶官不邇聲
色不殖貨利之說進者是欲
上爲禹湯也有以罔遊于逸罔淫于樂任賢勿
貳去邪勿疑之說進者是欲
上爲堯舜也夫欲致其君爲堯舜禹湯文武者
忠之大者也其君聽而用之成其臣爲皐
===
陶伊傅周召者聖之至者也然必臣止於
敬而後可以感其君之敬故曰惟大人爲
能格其君心夫臣以敬格君而君又以敬
自格是所謂咸有一德也由是前後左右
罔非正人而出入起居罔有不欽則長夜
之屏不足箴千秋之鑑祇爲贅耳如君心
未格而曰我善論思豈愚所敢信乎蠡管
之見若此惟執事可否之
第二問
punctuated:
之績，以無愧於儒者功用之全，則諸臣之責也。是故有以「玩人喪德，玩物喪志，敬勝怠，義勝欲」之說進者，是欲上爲文武也；有以「無敎逸欲，無曠庶官，不邇聲色，不殖貨利」之說進者，是欲上爲禹湯也；有以「罔遊于逸，罔淫于樂，任賢勿貳，去邪勿疑」之說進者，是欲上爲堯舜也。夫欲致其君爲堯舜禹湯文武者，忠之大者也；其君聽而用之，成其臣爲皐陶伊傅周召者，聖之至者也。然必臣止於敬，而後可以感其君之敬。故曰：「惟大人爲能格其君心。」夫臣以敬格君，而君又以敬自格，是所謂咸有一德也。由是前後左右罔非正人，而出入起居罔有不欽，則長夜之屏不足箴，千秋之鑑祇爲贅耳。如君心未格，而曰我善論思，豈愚所敢信乎？蠡管之見若此，惟執事可否之。

第二問
translation_en:
…their achievements, so as to live up to the full measure of what Confucian scholars can accomplish: this is the responsibility of the ministers. Thus, those who present the teachings, “Treating people as playthings destroys virtue; delighting in objects destroys resolve; reverence overcomes indolence, and righteousness overcomes desire,” wish His Majesty to become like Kings Wen and Wu. Those who present the teachings, “Do not encourage ease and desire; leave none of the offices unattended; do not draw near to music and sensual pleasures; do not accumulate wealth and profit,” wish His Majesty to become like Yu and Tang. Those who present the teachings, “Do not wander in idleness or indulge excessively in pleasure; appoint the worthy without wavering, and remove the wicked without hesitation,” wish His Majesty to become like Yao and Shun. To seek to make one’s ruler like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu is loyalty at its greatest. For the ruler to heed and employ these teachings, thereby enabling his ministers to become like Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, is sageliness at its utmost.

Yet ministers must first abide in reverence before they can stir reverence in their ruler. Hence the saying: “Only a great man can rectify his ruler’s heart.” When ministers rectify the ruler through reverence, and the ruler likewise rectifies himself through reverence, this is what is meant by “all possessing one virtue.” Consequently, those before and behind him, to his left and right, will all be upright people, and in going out and coming in, rising and resting, he will never fail to show reverence. Then the screen bearing the admonition against prolonged nocturnal revelry will have nothing to reprove, and the Mirror for a Thousand Autumns will merely be superfluous. If the ruler’s heart remains unrectified, yet someone says, “I am skilled in deliberation and reflection,” how could I, in my ignorance, venture to believe him? Such is my narrow view, like measuring the sea with a ladle or looking through a tube. I ask you, honored examiners, to judge whether it is acceptable.

Second Question

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
黃雲繪
同考試官教諭伍批我
皇上好生之德與天地竝中外臣工咸思祗承
德意躋斯世於仁壽之域子能悉心敷陳有欽若之意焉宜錄以獻
同考試官教諭鄭批我
皇上停刑肆赦與古帝王欽恤同心是篇得大意而闡揚之末復以持平責
文法吏其達於弼教之義者矣
考試官教授吳批以欽恤頌
聖德以平恕責有司皆確論也取之
===
考試官教授李批以仁義竝言得明刑之㫖
帝王之治天下也德可以化民乎曰可然
從違順逆之異齊君子不容不正之以義
法可以齊民乎曰可然輕重出入之異致
君子不容不濟之以仁夫惟義有所當執
是法有不可廢者由是設刑而威不軌以
濟仁之不及則民見義而懷刑夫惟仁有
所當施是情有所可原者由是原情而宥
無辜以節義之太過則民蒙仁而懷德故
punctuated:
黃雲繪

同考試官教諭伍批：我皇上好生之德，與天地竝，中外臣工咸思祗承德意，躋斯世於仁壽之域。子能悉心敷陳，有欽若之意焉，宜錄以獻。

同考試官教諭鄭批：我皇上停刑肆赦，與古帝王欽恤同心。是篇得大意而闡揚之，末復以持平責文法吏，其達於弼教之義者矣。

考試官教授吳批：以欽恤頌聖德，以平恕責有司，皆確論也，取之。

考試官教授李批：以仁義竝言，得明刑之㫖。

帝王之治天下也，德可以化民乎？曰：可。然從違順逆之異齊，君子不容不正之以義。法可以齊民乎？曰：可。然輕重出入之異致，君子不容不濟之以仁。夫惟義有所當執，是法有不可廢者。由是設刑而威不軌，以濟仁之不及，則民見義而懷刑。夫惟仁有所當施，是情有所可原者。由是原情而宥無辜，以節義之太過，則民蒙仁而懷德。故
translation_en:
Huang Yunhui

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: “Our Emperor’s virtue of cherishing life stands alongside that of Heaven and Earth. Officials at court and in the provinces all seek reverently to carry out his virtuous intentions and bring this age into a realm of benevolence and longevity. You have expounded this with full attention, showing a spirit of reverent compliance. This should be transcribed and presented.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “Our Emperor’s suspension of punishments and granting of pardons express the same reverent concern for those facing punishment as that of the ancient emperors and kings. This essay grasps and elucidates the main principle. At its close, it further charges officials who administer the written law with maintaining impartiality. Its author indeed understands the principle that punishment assists moral instruction.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: “It praises the imperial virtue for its reverent concern in punishment and charges the responsible officials with impartiality and forbearance. These are all sound arguments. Accept it.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: “By discussing benevolence and righteousness together, it grasps the purport of making punishments clear.”

When emperors and kings govern all under Heaven, can virtue transform the people? The answer is: it can. Yet, given the differences between compliance and disobedience, submission and defiance [?], the gentleman cannot fail to correct them through righteousness. Can law bring the people into order? The answer is: it can. Yet, given the differing consequences of lighter and heavier penalties, and of imposing or remitting punishment, the gentleman cannot fail to temper it with benevolence. Precisely because righteousness has principles that must be upheld, there are laws that cannot be set aside. Thus punishments are established to deter the lawless and supplement what benevolence cannot accomplish; the people then behold righteousness and hold punishment in mind. Precisely because benevolence has occasions on which it must be exercised, there are circumstances that warrant pardon. Thus circumstances are examined and the innocent are pardoned, to restrain excess in the application of righteousness; the people then receive benevolence and cherish virtue. Therefore…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
仁可過也義不可過也書曰眚災肆赦又
曰罪疑惟輕蓋聖人之心惟恐殺一不辜
以傷天地之和也嗚呼用刑豈聖人所獲
已也哉知乎此則我
聖祖欽恤之仁與
皇上好生之德所以保合太和以仁壽斯世者
真同符于唐虞三代正中外臣工所宜惟
明惟允將奉
德意以無負於
===
===
熈時者也請因明問而敬陳之昔者聖人之畫
卦也於震下離上而噬嗑名焉象曰雷電
噬嗑先王以明罰勅法此聖人以法輔治
之義也於離下艮上爲賁象曰山下有火
賁君子以明庶政無敢折獄此聖人尚德
緩刑之仁也然於赦過宥罪則象諸解議
獄緩死則象諸中孚焉其至誠惻怛之心
欽恤哀矜之念可槩見矣是故舜以玄德
帝於虞有士師之命矣然欽哉惟恤而天
punctuated:
仁可過也，義不可過也。《書》曰：「眚災肆赦。」又曰：「罪疑惟輕。」蓋聖人之心，惟恐殺一不辜，以傷天地之和也。嗚呼！用刑豈聖人所獲已也哉？知乎此，則我聖祖欽恤之仁與皇上好生之德，所以保合太和，以仁壽斯世者，真同符于唐虞三代，正中外臣工所宜惟明惟允，將奉德意，以無負於熈時者也。
請因明問而敬陳之。昔者聖人之畫卦也，於震下離上而噬嗑名焉。《象》曰：「雷電，噬嗑。先王以明罰勅法。」此聖人以法輔治之義也。於離下艮上爲賁，《象》曰：「山下有火，賁。君子以明庶政，無敢折獄。」此聖人尚德緩刑之仁也。然於赦過宥罪，則象諸解；議獄緩死，則象諸中孚焉。其至誠惻怛之心、欽恤哀矜之念，可槩見矣。是故舜以玄德帝於虞，有士師之命矣。然「欽哉惟恤」，而天
translation_en:
…benevolence may go beyond due measure, but righteousness must not. The Book of Documents says, “Pardon inadvertent faults and misfortunes,” and again, “When guilt is doubtful, favor the lighter penalty.” The sage’s heart fears above all that putting even one innocent person to death might injure the harmony of Heaven and Earth. Alas! Could imposing punishments be anything the sage could avoid? Understanding this, we see that the benevolence of our Sagely Ancestor in exercising reverent care in punishment, together with His Majesty’s virtue in cherishing life, preserves supreme harmony and brings this age benevolence and longevity. These truly accord with the ways of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. Officials at court and throughout the realm should therefore exercise discernment and fairness, respectfully carrying out this virtuous intent so as not to fail this flourishing age.
Permit me to respond to your illuminating question by respectfully setting forth the matter. When the sages of old drew the hexagrams, they named the one with Zhen below and Li above Shihe, “Biting Through.” The Commentary on the Images says: “Thunder and lightning: Biting Through. The former kings thereby clarified punishments and put the laws in order.” This expresses the sages’ righteousness in using law to assist government. With Li below and Gen above, the hexagram is Bi, “Adornment.” The Commentary on the Images says: “Fire beneath the mountain: Adornment. The gentleman thereby brings clarity to the affairs of government, but does not venture to decide criminal cases.” This expresses the sages’ benevolence in esteeming virtue and tempering punishment. For pardoning faults and forgiving offenses, they took their image from Xie, “Release”; for deliberating on criminal cases and delaying executions, they took their image from Zhongfu, “Inner Sincerity.” Here one can broadly discern their utterly sincere and compassionate hearts, and their concern for reverent care, pity, and mercy in punishment. Thus Shun, through his profound virtue, ruled as emperor in Yu and issued an appointment to the Judge. Yet he enjoined, “Be reverent! Be compassionate!” and all under Heaven…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
下咸服恩何渥耶禹以台德王於夏有常
刑之制矣然下車泣罪而兆民允懷仁何
溥耶成康業承于文武法備於周官則有
大司寇以掌邦禁以兩造禁民訟以兩劑
禁民獄及大司徒所掌八刑以糾萬民亦
旣詳且密矣然猶懼愚民之陷於罪也于
是詳之以五聽訊之以三刺原之以三赦
三宥而愼獄敬刑之訓靄然忠厚之家法
焉其後百姓免於刑戮興於禮義而囹圄
===
空虛者孰非仁心仁政之所培植也哉夫
四君者好生之德旣洽於勅法之先而不
忍之心每周於得情之後何曾輕議一辟
以損乎惻隱之仁此太和元氣在虞夏成
周宇宙間者信不誣矣周澤旣衰法令滋
起申韓馳騁於戰國斯高睚眦於嬴秦誹
謗者族誅偶語者棄市刑威熾而忠恕薄
無足論者嗣漢而下高帝約法三章文帝
詔除肉刑非不足以聯屬人心稱漢令主
punctuated:
下咸服，恩何渥耶！禹以台德王於夏，有常刑之制矣。然下車泣罪，而兆民允懷，仁何溥耶！成康業承于文武，法備於周官，則有大司寇以掌邦禁，以兩造禁民訟，以兩劑禁民獄，及大司徒所掌八刑以糾萬民，亦旣詳且密矣。然猶懼愚民之陷於罪也，于是詳之以五聽，訊之以三刺，原之以三赦三宥，而愼獄敬刑之訓，靄然忠厚之家法焉。其後百姓免於刑戮，興於禮義，而囹圄空虛者，孰非仁心仁政之所培植也哉！夫四君者，好生之德旣洽於勅法之先，而不忍之心每周於得情之後，何曾輕議一辟，以損乎惻隱之仁？此太和元氣在虞夏成周宇宙間者，信不誣矣。

周澤旣衰，法令滋起。申韓馳騁於戰國，斯高睚眦於嬴秦，誹謗者族誅，偶語者棄市，刑威熾而忠恕薄，無足論者。嗣漢而下，高帝約法三章，文帝詔除肉刑，非不足以聯屬人心，稱漢令主
translation_en:
…all under Heaven submitted. How abundant was his grace! Yu ruled as king in Xia through his virtue [?], and established a system of regular punishments. Yet he descended from his carriage and wept over an offender, and the myriad people sincerely cherished him. How all-embracing was his benevolence! Kings Cheng and Kang inherited the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, and their laws were fully set out in the Offices of Zhou. There was the Minister of Justice, who administered the prohibitions of the realm, regulated the people's civil suits by requiring both parties to appear, and regulated their criminal cases by requiring the two written pleadings. There were also the eight punishments administered by the Minister of Education to correct the myriad people. These arrangements were already detailed and thorough. Yet they still feared that ignorant people would fall into crime. Thus they examined cases carefully through the five modes of hearing evidence, investigated them through the three consultations, and considered grounds for clemency through the three exemptions and three mitigations. Their injunctions to exercise caution in adjudication and reverence in punishment breathed the spirit of a loyal and generous dynastic tradition. Subsequently, the common people escaped punishment and execution, flourished in ritual propriety and righteousness, and the prisons stood empty. Which of these results was not nurtured by benevolent hearts and benevolent government? These four rulers' virtue of cherishing life was already pervasive before they put the laws in order, and their hearts, unable to bear others' suffering, invariably extended compassion after the facts had been established. When did they ever lightly deliberate upon a single punishment, thereby impairing their compassionate benevolence? That the primordial vital force of supreme harmony filled the world under Yu, Xia, and the flourishing Zhou is indeed no false claim.

Once Zhou's beneficent influence declined, laws and ordinances multiplied. Shen Buhai and Han Fei held sway in the Warring States, while Li Si and Zhao Gao pursued vindictive grudges under the Qin of the Ying house. Those who voiced criticism were executed together with their clans; those who conversed in pairs were executed in the marketplace. The terror of punishment blazed, while conscientiousness and consideration for others dwindled: such men hardly merit discussion. From the succeeding Han onward, Emperor Gao reduced the laws to three articles, and Emperor Wen decreed the abolition of mutilating punishments. These measures were certainly sufficient to bind the people's hearts together and earn them recognition as worthy rulers of Han…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
也然韓彭葅醢不免於寡恩薄昭伏誅則
失於慎始其後再傳而至武宣張湯趙禹
之徒進故縱連坐之法行一則繁刑多殺
一則啓釁基禍而漢家元氣剗削無餘可
勝嘆哉唐太宗奏必五覆幾致刑措矣然
君羨以圖讖含寃蘊古以直言被戮揆法
得無濫乎未幾而孽后司晨周興等盛開
告密致宗室大臣咸肝腦於酷吏之手夫
豈明刑之中也哉宋太宗親錄繫囚用法
===
平恕矣然武功以危疑自盡涪陵以私憾
貶死反巳寧無慚乎數傳而煕豐變法章
惇等恣為巧詆俾正人君子咸羅織於奸
黨之門夫豈貽謀之善也哉斯四君者或
狃於秦漢之習或溺於好惡之偏又安望
其恤民命致天和與前聖相脗合耶洪惟
我
太祖高皇帝以萬世綱常之主拯胡元憔悴之
民首命刑部尚書劉惟謙等重定諸律而
punctuated:
也。然韓彭葅醢，不免於寡恩；薄昭伏誅，則失於慎始。其後再傳而至武宣，張湯、趙禹之徒進，故縱連坐之法行。一則繁刑多殺，一則啓釁基禍，而漢家元氣剗削無餘，可勝嘆哉！唐太宗奏必五覆，幾致刑措矣。然君羨以圖讖含寃，蘊古以直言被戮，揆法得無濫乎？未幾而孽后司晨，周興等盛開告密，致宗室大臣咸肝腦於酷吏之手，夫豈明刑之中也哉？宋太宗親錄繫囚，用法平恕矣。然武功以危疑自盡，涪陵以私憾貶死，反巳寧無慚乎？數傳而煕豐變法，章惇等恣為巧詆，俾正人君子咸羅織於奸黨之門，夫豈貽謀之善也哉？斯四君者，或狃於秦漢之習，或溺於好惡之偏，又安望其恤民命、致天和，與前聖相脗合耶？
洪惟我太祖高皇帝，以萬世綱常之主，拯胡元憔悴之民，首命刑部尚書劉惟謙等重定諸律，而
translation_en:
…indeed. Yet the mincing and pickling of Han Xin and Peng Yue betrayed a lack of benevolence; the execution of Bo Zhao showed a failure to exercise caution at the outset. After two further successions came Emperors Wu and Xuan. Men such as Zhang Tang and Zhao Yu rose to prominence, and laws concerning deliberate release of offenders and collective liability were put into effect. One multiplied punishments and executions; the other opened the way to conflict and laid the foundations of disaster. The vital strength of the Han ruling house was stripped away entirely. How could one lament this enough!
Emperor Taizong of Tang required five reviews of capital sentences submitted to him and nearly achieved a state in which punishments could be set aside. Yet Junxian suffered injustice because of a prophetic text, and Yungu was put to death for speaking frankly. Judged against the law, were these not excessive punishments? Before long, a wicked empress usurped authority, like a hen announcing the dawn. Zhou Xing and others threw open the channels for secret denunciations, causing imperial clansmen and high ministers alike to perish brutally at the hands of cruel officials. How could this represent the proper balance in making punishments clear?
Emperor Taizong of Song personally reviewed prisoners’ cases and applied the law impartially and leniently. Yet Wugong took his own life amid peril and suspicion, while Fuling was demoted out of a private grudge and died. Could the emperor have reflected on himself without shame? Several reigns later came the reforms of the Xining and Yuanfeng eras. Zhang Dun and others freely contrived accusations, ensnaring upright men and gentlemen in charges of belonging to a treacherous faction. How could this be called sound planning for posterity? These four rulers were either habituated to the practices of Qin and Han or submerged in partiality arising from their likes and dislikes. How could one expect them to cherish the people’s lives and bring about Heaven’s harmony, in accord with the sages of old?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, as the sovereign who established the cardinal bonds and enduring norms for ten thousand generations, rescued the people worn down under the non-Han Yuan. He first commanded Liu Weiqian, Minister of Justice, and others to revise the statutes, and…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
近代比例可資奸吏出入者咸痛革之緣
情定制務協厥中蓋唐宋以來所未有者
也及伏讀
祖訓一書申嚴大明律誥之守禁用黥刺剕劓
之刑至於
戒諭憲臣又有論法不當必傷善類之詞有
用藥或誤必致戕生之喻又曰鞫獄當平
恕自今民犯者毋連坐又曰善為國者惟
以好生樹德不以刑殺立威大哉
===
聖謨所以欽恤羣黎貽謀
億代者一何至也故仁心仁政浹洽於海宇
二百年來刑當其罪民安其生有由然矣
迨我
皇上以聰明仁聖之資撫
重熙累洽之運赦宥之條旣頒於
登極明詔矣茲當天下審决之期復
俞言官停免之請是心也卽天地好生之心也
舜禹成康欽恤之心也其與
punctuated:
近代比例可資奸吏出入者，咸痛革之，緣情定制，務協厥中，蓋唐宋以來所未有者也。及伏讀《祖訓》一書，申嚴《大明律誥》之守，禁用黥刺剕劓之刑。至於戒諭憲臣，又有「論法不當，必傷善類」之詞，有「用藥或誤，必致戕生」之喻。又曰：「鞫獄當平恕，自今民犯者毋連坐。」又曰：「善為國者，惟以好生樹德，不以刑殺立威。」大哉聖謨！所以欽恤羣黎、貽謀億代者，一何至也！故仁心仁政浹洽於海宇，二百年來，刑當其罪，民安其生，有由然矣。

迨我皇上以聰明仁聖之資，撫重熙累洽之運，赦宥之條旣頒於登極明詔矣。茲當天下審决之期，復俞言官停免之請。是心也，卽天地好生之心也，舜禹成康欽恤之心也，其與
translation_en:
…and thoroughly abolished all recent precedents and analogical rulings that corrupt officials could exploit to manipulate convictions and acquittals. He established regulations with regard to the circumstances, striving to attain the proper balance—something not seen since the Tang and Song dynasties. Moreover, when we reverently read the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun), we find strict insistence on observance of the Great Ming Code and Grand Pronouncements, and a prohibition on punishments involving tattooing, cutting off the feet, or cutting off the nose. His admonitions to censorial officials also include the words, “Improper application of the law will inevitably harm good people,” and the analogy, “An error in administering medicine will inevitably destroy life.” He further said, “In trying cases, be impartial and merciful. Henceforth, when commoners commit offenses, do not implicate others through collective liability.” Again he said, “Those who govern a state well establish virtue through cherishing life; they do not establish authority through punishment and execution.” How great were these sagely counsels! How consummate his care and compassion for the common people and his provision for countless generations! Thus his benevolent heart and benevolent government permeated the entire realm. For two hundred years, punishments have fitted offenses and the people have lived in security: there is good reason for this.

Now Our Emperor, endowed with intelligence, benevolence, and sageliness, presides over an age of successive brilliance and accumulated harmony. Provisions for pardon and clemency have already been promulgated in the illustrious edict marking his accession. Now, at the time for reviewing cases and carrying out executions throughout the realm, he has again approved the request of the remonstrance officials to suspend or remit executions. This heart is the very heart of Heaven and Earth that cherishes life, the heart of Shun, Yu, and Kings Cheng and Kang that exercises reverent care and compassion in punishment. In relation to…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
皇祖慈祥之訓先後一揆故中外臣民躬逢
聖澤喜獲甦生莫不欣欣然歌詠太平矣有
君如此奚忍負之夫
恩詔渙頒其所以奉行者罔敢豫怠矣但
德意隆盛而推廣者庸有未周是故由憲臣以
及有司教以禮讓斷獄大減如韓延壽者
固不無其人矣然畫地不入刻木不對得
無如路溫舒之論於漢者乎獨存平恕不
施鞭朴如徐有功者固不無其人矣然失
===
入無辜失出為大罪得無如劉德威之論
於唐者乎至如緝捕以懲奸慝也乃今平
民瘐於鍛鍊一眚窮於文致即
輦轂之下猶或有冤者况閭閻之遠者乎笞
杖本屬輕刑也乃今榜笞烈於炮烙性命
殞於箠楚即內郡之臣猶或不免焉况荒
僻之陬乎夫匹夫結憤六月飛霜一婦含
冤三年不雨刑罰僭忒關係匪輕而苛吏
虐民者奚容於
punctuated: 皇祖慈祥之訓，先後一揆。故中外臣民躬逢聖澤，喜獲甦生，莫不欣欣然歌詠太平矣。有君如此，奚忍負之？夫恩詔渙頒，其所以奉行者罔敢豫怠矣。但德意隆盛，而推廣者庸有未周。是故由憲臣以及有司，教以禮讓，斷獄大減，如韓延壽者，固不無其人矣。然畫地不入，刻木不對，得無如路溫舒之論於漢者乎？獨存平恕，不施鞭朴，如徐有功者，固不無其人矣。然失入無辜，失出為大罪，得無如劉德威之論於唐者乎？至如緝捕以懲奸慝也，乃今平民瘐於鍛鍊，一眚窮於文致，即輦轂之下猶或有冤者，况閭閻之遠者乎？笞杖本屬輕刑也，乃今榜笞烈於炮烙，性命殞於箠楚，即內郡之臣猶或不免焉，况荒僻之陬乎？夫匹夫結憤，六月飛霜；一婦含冤，三年不雨。刑罰僭忒，關係匪輕，而苛吏虐民者奚容於
translation_en:
…accords in every respect with the compassionate instructions of the imperial ancestor, earlier and later alike. Thus officials and common people, at court and throughout the realm, personally receiving the imperial grace and rejoicing at their renewed lease on life, all joyfully sing the praises of peace. With such a ruler, how could anyone bear to fail him? Now that the gracious edict has been widely promulgated, none charged with carrying it out dares be lax. Yet, abundant though this benevolent intent is, its extension may still fall short of completeness.

Among the censorial officials and local authorities, there are certainly men like Han Yanshou, who teach ritual propriety and deference and thereby greatly reduce the cases requiring judgment. Yet people will not enter even a prison traced on the ground, nor answer even a wooden likeness of a prison official: might the situation still resemble what Lu Wenshu described under the Han? There are certainly men like Xu Yougong, who uphold impartiality and forbearance alone and do not wield whips or rods. Yet innocent people are wrongly convicted, while mistaken acquittals are treated as grave crimes: might the situation still resemble what Liu Dewei described under the Tang?

As for pursuing and arresting offenders, this is intended to punish wickedness. Yet today ordinary people languish in prison under fabricated charges, and a single fault brings utter ruin through the tendentious construction of a case. Even at the foot of the imperial carriage—in the capital itself—some still suffer injustice; how much more so in distant villages? Beating with the light or heavy bamboo is originally classed as a light punishment. Yet today flogging is fiercer than burning with heated bronze, and lives are lost beneath the rods. Even officials in the interior commanderies sometimes cannot escape this fate; how much more so in remote and desolate corners?

When a single man harbored bitter resentment, frost fell in the sixth month; when one woman suffered injustice, no rain fell for three years. Excesses and errors in punishment have consequences of no small gravity. How, then, can harsh officials who abuse the people be tolerated in…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
堯舜之世哉玆欲刑期無刑辟以止辟廣
皇仁以凝
天命宣惠政以恢
帝業當如何而後可亦曰重敎化清淹獄明律
例愼簡任而已夫帝舜之命契曰敬敷五
敎在寬其命皐陶曰明于五刑以弼五敎
則敎固刑之本也故必樹之軌則導之典
禮以啓其忠信之心以防其邪僻之念其
有不率敎者然後齊之以刑焉則民安於
===
爲善恥於犯法而比閭鮮爭鬭之獄矣崇
敎非所先乎夫夏月錄囚輕罪隨卽决遣
未能决者出獄聽候此
祖宗之恤典恩至厚也今各省有會審之例三
年有恤刑之官法亦備矣但郡縣獄犴每
遇天氣炎蒸之日類多病疫待斃之囚是
宜著爲令甲通行監司郡縣每年依期淸
審輕罪如律决遣毋致久淹則囹圄無坐
斃之民矣淸獄非所急乎夫罪有輕重吏
punctuated:
堯舜之世哉！玆欲刑期無刑，辟以止辟，廣皇仁以凝天命，宣惠政以恢帝業，當如何而後可？亦曰重敎化、清淹獄、明律例、愼簡任而已。
夫帝舜之命契曰：「敬敷五敎，在寬。」其命皐陶曰：「明于五刑，以弼五敎。」則敎固刑之本也。故必樹之軌則，導之典禮，以啓其忠信之心，以防其邪僻之念。其有不率敎者，然後齊之以刑焉，則民安於爲善，恥於犯法，而比閭鮮爭鬭之獄矣。崇敎非所先乎？
夫夏月錄囚，輕罪隨卽决遣，未能决者出獄聽候，此祖宗之恤典，恩至厚也。今各省有會審之例，三年有恤刑之官，法亦備矣。但郡縣獄犴，每遇天氣炎蒸之日，類多病疫待斃之囚。是宜著爲令甲，通行監司郡縣，每年依期淸審，輕罪如律决遣，毋致久淹，則囹圄無坐斃之民矣。淸獄非所急乎？夫罪有輕重，吏
translation_en:
…in the age of Yao and Shun! Now, if we wish to employ punishment with the aim of dispensing with punishment, and penalties to put an end to penalties; to extend imperial benevolence so as to secure Heaven’s Mandate, and to promulgate beneficent government so as to enlarge the imperial enterprise—how can this be achieved? Simply by giving weight to moral instruction, clearing protracted imprisonment, clarifying the statutes and substatutes, and exercising care in selecting and appointing officials.
When Emperor Shun charged Xie, he said: “Reverently spread the five teachings, doing so with leniency.” When he charged Gao Yao, he said: “Be discerning in applying the five punishments, thereby supporting the five teachings.” Thus moral instruction is indeed the foundation of punishment. We must therefore establish standards for the people and guide them through prescribed rites, awakening their loyalty and trustworthiness and guarding against wayward and depraved thoughts. Only those who fail to follow this instruction should then be brought into conformity through punishment. The people will thus find contentment in doing good and feel shame at breaking the law, and neighborhoods will have few cases arising from quarrels and fighting. Is promoting moral instruction not the first priority?
In the summer months, prisoners’ cases are reviewed: those charged with minor offenses are promptly sentenced and discharged, while those whose cases cannot yet be decided are released from prison to await a hearing. This compassionate provision of our imperial ancestors is an act of profound benevolence. At present, each province has provisions for joint judicial review, and every three years officials are assigned to review punishments with a view to clemency. The legal arrangements are thus comprehensive. Yet in prefectural and county prisons, whenever the weather becomes sweltering, there are commonly many prisoners suffering from disease and epidemics, awaiting death. It is therefore fitting to establish a formal ordinance and circulate it to the surveillance authorities, prefectures, and counties, requiring them to conduct thorough reviews at the prescribed time each year. Those guilty of minor offenses should be sentenced and discharged according to law, without prolonged detention. Then no one will die merely from languishing in prison. Is clearing the prisons not an urgent task? Offenses differ in gravity, and officials…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
有愛憎所欲活者傅生議所欲陷者比死
刑是受賕者得枉法以惠奸非辜者以深
文而抵罪即能控訴以自明然摩頂放踵
已不勝其荼毒矣謂宜申明律例如科條
未備者則爲之詳定其倫要如文義未明
者則爲之考訂其亂辭以頒布中外咸使
欽遵仍
勅諭問刑衙門凡有律例重而情狀輕者不得
妄行比附則法律畫一輕重有程而深刻
===
之吏又安得舞文操切耶夫張釋之爲廷
尉天下無寃民于定國爲廷尉民自以不
寃言在得人也今之獄吏擇之不可不精
任之不可不久察之不可不嚴是在撫按
督監司監司察守令其折獄明允蔚有仁
聲者則增秩賜金以責其成效然後破格
超遷以風勵乎庶職而乳虎蒼鷹羅鉗吉
網者即貶黜而重治之勿俾夤緣倖免則
守令皆循良而慘酷之吏又安得殘民以
punctuated: 有愛憎，所欲活者傅生議，所欲陷者比死刑，是受賕者得枉法以惠奸，非辜者以深文而抵罪。即能控訴以自明，然摩頂放踵，已不勝其荼毒矣。謂宜申明律例，如科條未備者，則爲之詳定其倫要；如文義未明者，則爲之考訂其亂辭，以頒布中外，咸使欽遵。仍勅諭問刑衙門，凡有律例重而情狀輕者，不得妄行比附，則法律畫一，輕重有程，而深刻之吏又安得舞文操切耶？夫張釋之爲廷尉，天下無寃民；于定國爲廷尉，民自以不寃，言在得人也。今之獄吏，擇之不可不精，任之不可不久，察之不可不嚴。是在撫按督監司，監司察守令。其折獄明允、蔚有仁聲者，則增秩賜金，以責其成效，然後破格超遷，以風勵乎庶職；而乳虎蒼鷹、羅鉗吉網者，即貶黜而重治之，勿俾夤緣倖免。則守令皆循良，而慘酷之吏又安得殘民以
translation_en:
…have their likes and dislikes. For those they wish to keep alive, they adduce arguments for sparing life; for those they wish to entrap, they apply capital punishment by analogy. Thus bribe-takers can pervert the law to favor wrongdoers, while innocent people are convicted through strained interpretations of the law. Even if they can lodge complaints and clear themselves, they have already been worn down from head to heel and subjected to unbearable suffering. I submit that the statutes and substatutes should be clarified. Where provisions are incomplete, their organization and essentials [?] should be established in detail; where the wording is unclear, its confused expressions [?] should be examined and corrected. These should then be promulgated at court and throughout the provinces, so that all may respectfully comply. An imperial command should also instruct the offices adjudicating criminal cases that whenever the statutory penalty is severe but the circumstances are comparatively minor, they must not recklessly apply provisions by analogy. The laws would then be uniform, with established standards for the severity of punishment. How could harsh officials continue manipulating legal language and dealing oppressively with people?

When Zhang Shizhi served as Chamberlain for Law Enforcement, there were no people under heaven who suffered injustice; when Yu Dingguo held that office, the people themselves felt that they suffered no injustice. This means that everything depends upon obtaining the right men. In selecting judicial officials today, one must exercise the utmost care; their tenure must be sufficiently long, and scrutiny of their conduct must be strict. It falls to the grand coordinators and regional inspectors to supervise the surveillance officials, and to the surveillance officials to scrutinize the prefects and magistrates. Those who decide cases clearly and fairly and enjoy a flourishing reputation for benevolence should receive increases in rank and gifts of money, holding them accountable for results. Thereafter they should receive exceptional, accelerated promotion, to encourage officials in all posts. But those who behave like tigresses with cubs or fierce hawks, employing the pincers of Luo and the nets of Ji—devices for entrapping people—should immediately be demoted or dismissed and severely punished. They must not be allowed to escape through connections or good fortune. Prefects and magistrates would then all be conscientious and benevolent. How could cruel officials still ravage the people in order to…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
逞哉脩此四者則刑罰中而民心不惑聽
讞審而訟獄稱平肺石無畫籲之冤乾膚
得金矢之宜其所以擴
皇上好生之德而漸致刑措之治者豈淺淺哉
雖然猶有本焉書曰民心罔中惟爾之中
爾身克正罔敢不正孔子曰道之以德齊
之以禮有耻且格惟願我
皇上於端拱清穆之際切望道未見之誠主敬
以存此心務學以明此心親近君子以維
===
持此心則心正而身克脩矣由是正身以
正
朝廷以正百官以正萬民將見在朝成師讓
之風在野協雍睦之化德教行而獄訟銷
自可措刑於不用矣此固端本澄源之道
竊有望於
今日者也惟執事采而行之幸甚
第三問
魏良臣
punctuated:
逞哉？脩此四者，則刑罰中而民心不惑，聽讞審而訟獄稱平，肺石無畫籲之冤，乾膚得金矢之宜。其所以擴皇上好生之德，而漸致刑措之治者，豈淺淺哉！雖然，猶有本焉。《書》曰：「民心罔中，惟爾之中。爾身克正，罔敢不正。」孔子曰：「道之以德，齊之以禮，有耻且格。」惟願我皇上於端拱清穆之際，切望道未見之誠，主敬以存此心，務學以明此心，親近君子以維持此心，則心正而身克脩矣。由是正身，以正朝廷，以正百官，以正萬民，將見在朝成師讓之風，在野協雍睦之化。德教行而獄訟銷，自可措刑於不用矣。此固端本澄源之道，竊有望於今日者也。惟執事采而行之，幸甚！

第三問

魏良臣
translation_en:
…give vent to their cruelty? If these four measures are put into practice, punishments will be fitting and the people's hearts will not be bewildered; hearings and judicial deliberations will be thorough, and litigation and criminal cases will be judged fairly. At the lung-stone, where grievances are brought, there will be no injustices prompting appeals [?]; the requirements for submitting dried meat and metal arrowheads as pledges in lawsuits will be properly observed. Could these measures make only a slight contribution to extending His Majesty's virtue of cherishing life and gradually achieving a government in which punishments are laid aside?

Yet there is still a fundamental principle. The Documents says: “The people's hearts have no constant mean; they take your mean as their own. If your person is truly upright, none will dare to be otherwise.” Confucius said: “Guide them through virtue and bring them into accord through ritual: they will have a sense of shame and will set themselves right.” I ask only that, while His Majesty sits with folded hands in serene dignity, he earnestly sustain the sincerity of one who longs for the Way as though he had not yet seen it; make reverence his guiding principle to preserve this heart; apply himself to learning to illuminate this heart; and draw near to exemplary men to sustain this heart. Then his heart will be upright and his person duly cultivated. By rectifying himself, he will thus rectify the court, the hundred officials, and the myriad people. We shall then see a spirit of mutual respect and deference [?] established at court, and harmonious transformation among the people. Once moral instruction prevails and litigation disappears, punishments can naturally be laid aside unused. This is indeed the way to set the root right and cleanse the source, and it is what I humbly hope for today. If you, the officials responsible, would adopt and implement these proposals, I would count it a great blessing!

Third Question

Wei Liangchen

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭鄭批古今無不弊之法是在人
究極弊源變而通之耳經生遂能及此有用之學也錄之
同考試官教授何批愼選舉公考課治天下之大端
也子能鑒古籌今早有定見殆匹夫而懷當世之慮者耶
考試官教授吳批通達治體宜錄以式
考試官教授李批博洽之學練達之才
賢才國家之利器也雖有良工器弗利則
無以善其事雖有明主賢弗用則罔與成
厥功甚哉賢才之有關於人國也用賢之
===
道其始也不有以招徠之何以盡天下之
才其既也不有以甄别之何以成天下之
理是故養之欲豫擇之欲精則招徠之道
也辨之欲嚴核之欲實則甄别之術也擇
之精不才者不得以倖進核之實不肖者
不得以苟容持此以往而選舉考課之法
庶可以得真才圖實効而國家尚亦有利
矣執事發策而舉二法以為問愚也方挾
筴以就繩約何敢窺而議之雖然請誦所
punctuated:
同考試官教諭鄭批：古今無不弊之法，是在人究極弊源，變而通之耳。經生遂能及此有用之學也，錄之。

同考試官教授何批：愼選舉，公考課，治天下之大端也。子能鑒古籌今，早有定見，殆匹夫而懷當世之慮者耶？

考試官教授吳批：通達治體，宜錄以式。

考試官教授李批：博洽之學，練達之才。

賢才，國家之利器也。雖有良工，器弗利則無以善其事；雖有明主，賢弗用則罔與成厥功。甚哉，賢才之有關於人國也！用賢之道，其始也，不有以招徠之，何以盡天下之才？其既也，不有以甄别之，何以成天下之理？是故養之欲豫，擇之欲精，則招徠之道也；辨之欲嚴，核之欲實，則甄别之術也。擇之精，不才者不得以倖進；核之實，不肖者不得以苟容。持此以往，而選舉考課之法庶可以得真才，圖實効，而國家尚亦有利矣。執事發策而舉二法以為問，愚也方挾筴以就繩約，何敢窺而議之？雖然，請誦所
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Throughout history, no institution has been free from defects. It is simply for people to investigate the ultimate sources of those defects and make changes so that the institution can function effectively. That a student of the Classics should attain such useful learning! Accept this essay.

Comment by Associate Examiner He, Professor: Care in selecting and recommending men, and impartiality in evaluating officials’ performance, are fundamental to governing the realm. You can examine antiquity and deliberate upon the present, and have already formed definite views. Are you perhaps a commoner who nevertheless bears concern for the affairs of the age?

Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: A thorough understanding of the essentials of government; this should be selected as a model.

Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: Broad and comprehensive learning; seasoned and accomplished ability.

Worthy and talented men are the state’s sharp tools. Even with a skilled craftsman, if his tools are not sharp, he cannot do his work well; even with an enlightened ruler, if worthy men are not employed, he has no one with whom to accomplish his work. How profoundly worthy and talented men matter to a state! In employing worthy men, unless there are means to attract them at the outset, how can all the talent in the realm be brought into service? Once they have entered service, unless there are means to distinguish among them, how can good government throughout the realm be achieved? Thus, nurturing them in advance and selecting them carefully constitute the way to attract them; discriminating rigorously and assessing their actual performance constitute the method for distinguishing among them. When selection is careful, the untalented cannot advance through mere good fortune; when assessment rests on actual performance, the unworthy cannot retain their positions merely by getting by. By proceeding in this way, the institutions for selecting and recommending men and for evaluating officials’ performance may obtain true talent and achieve practical results, bringing benefit to the state.

You, honored examiners, have issued a policy question asking about these two institutions. I, in my ignorance, have only just come with my writing tablets to submit to the prescribed rules; how dare I presume to examine and discuss them? Nevertheless, allow me to recite what …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
聞以對夫天下可以一人有不可以一人
理書曰惟后非賢不乂言賢才之當用也
又曰知人則哲能官人言用人之當審也
惟用賢之爲急是故有選舉之法惟審用
之爲要是故有考課之法玆二法者其機
常相須而効實相因也無曠庶官天工人
其代之有功不賞有罪不罰雖堯舜不能
以爲理知乎此可以論治而語法矣選舉
之法何始乎自明揚師錫見於虞廷而求
===
賢之制其來遠矣然而莫備於周也周禮
大司徒以鄕三物敎萬民而賓興之三年
大比則合六鄕之民而考其德行道藝黨
正書之州長考之鄕大夫則以鄕飲酒禮
禮而賓之升之司徒升之司馬然後論定
而官焉其制詳且盡矣故一時得人稱爲
極盛而兎罝羔羊之咏非偶然也自是以
還漢詔郡國舉士之制不一而大槩有三
曰賢良方正也孝廉也博士弟子也賢良
punctuated:
聞以對。夫天下可以一人有，不可以一人理。《書》曰：「惟后非賢不乂。」言賢才之當用也。又曰：「知人則哲，能官人。」言用人之當審也。惟用賢之爲急，是故有選舉之法；惟審用之爲要，是故有考課之法。玆二法者，其機常相須，而効實相因也。「無曠庶官，天工人其代之。」「有功不賞，有罪不罰，雖堯舜不能以爲理。」知乎此，可以論治而語法矣。

選舉之法何始乎？自明揚師錫見於虞廷，而求賢之制其來遠矣。然而莫備於周也。《周禮》，大司徒以鄕三物敎萬民而賓興之。三年大比，則合六鄕之民而考其德行道藝。黨正書之，州長考之，鄕大夫則以鄕飲酒禮禮而賓之，升之司徒，升之司馬，然後論定而官焉。其制詳且盡矣。故一時得人稱爲極盛，而《兎罝》《羔羊》之咏非偶然也。自是以還，漢詔郡國舉士之制不一，而大槩有三：曰賢良方正也，孝廉也，博士弟子也。賢良
translation_en:
…what I have heard, by way of reply. All under Heaven may be possessed by one man, but cannot be governed by one man alone. The Book of Documents says: “The sovereign cannot bring about order without worthy men.” This means that worthy talent must be employed. It also says: “Knowing men constitutes wisdom, and enables one to appoint men to office.” This means that one must exercise discernment in employing men. Because employing the worthy is urgent, there are procedures for selection and recommendation; because discerning how to employ them is essential, there are procedures for evaluating officials. These two procedures always depend upon one another in their operation, and their results are likewise interdependent. “Let none of the many offices go unfilled: Heaven’s work is to be performed by men in its stead.” “If merit is not rewarded and wrongdoing is not punished, even Yao and Shun could not bring about order.” Understanding this, one can discuss government and its procedures.

Where did the procedures for selection and recommendation begin? From the time when the court of Shun openly sought out worthy men and received recommendations from the assembled officials, institutions for seeking the worthy have had a long history. Yet none were more comprehensive than those of the Zhou. According to the Rites of Zhou, the Minister of Education instructed the people in the three categories of township teaching and advanced the worthy, honoring them as guests. At the great triennial assessment, the people of the six townships were assembled and examined in virtue, conduct, learning, and skills. The Neighborhood Heads recorded their qualifications, the District Chiefs assessed them, and the Township Grand Masters honored them as guests at the township drinking ceremony. They were then advanced to the Minister of Education and to the Minister of War; only after deliberation and a final determination were they appointed to office. These arrangements were detailed and comprehensive. Thus the recruitment of capable men in that age was acclaimed as having reached its height, and the praises sung in “The Rabbit Net” and “The Lamb’s Fleece” were no accident. Thereafter, under the Han, imperial edicts established various procedures by which commanderies and kingdoms recommended men for service. Broadly speaking, there were three categories: the Worthy and Good, Upright and Correct; the Filial and Incorrupt; and students of the Erudites. The Worthy and Good…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
孝廉舉以任用若周官之進士博土弟子
入補國學若周官之俊士猶有德行之遺
意焉唐之科目雖多而行之最久者有二
曰明經也進士也進士以聲韻爲學不本
經術明經以帖誦爲能不窮義理所謂德
行者不復問矣宋初猶並用二科至王安
石乃盡廢諸科令士各占治易詩書周禮
禮記一經兼以論語孟子每試四場經義
以探其學術論策以考其智慮且曰欲以
===
一道德而同風俗也漢唐宋之法皆能得
人要而求之則宋中更之制有不可廢者
蓋漢制近古而今則難行唐制尚文而實
則未競宋則變聲律爲議論變墨義爲大
義而發策決科之士庶幾有誦聖賢之遺
言而窺其用心者此其法之可取也雖未
可方成周三物之教而後世之制則爲彼
善矣考課之法何始乎自敷奏明試之典
見於虞廷而課功之制其來遠矣然而莫
punctuated:
孝廉舉以任用，若周官之進士；博土弟子入補國學，若周官之俊士，猶有德行之遺意焉。唐之科目雖多，而行之最久者有二，曰明經也，進士也。進士以聲韻爲學，不本經術；明經以帖誦爲能，不窮義理。所謂德行者，不復問矣。宋初猶並用二科，至王安石乃盡廢諸科，令士各占治易、詩、書、周禮、禮記一經，兼以論語、孟子。每試四場，經義以探其學術，論策以考其智慮，且曰：「欲以一道德而同風俗也。」漢唐宋之法皆能得人，要而求之，則宋中更之制有不可廢者。蓋漢制近古，而今則難行；唐制尚文，而實則未競；宋則變聲律爲議論，變墨義爲大義，而發策決科之士，庶幾有誦聖賢之遺言而窺其用心者。此其法之可取也。雖未可方成周三物之教，而後世之制則爲彼善矣。

考課之法何始乎？自敷奏明試之典見於虞廷，而課功之制其來遠矣。然而莫
translation_en:
…those recommended as Filial and Incorrupt were selected for appointment, like the “presented scholars” in the Offices of Zhou; the disciples of the Erudites [?] entered the state school to fill its places, like the “outstanding scholars” in the Offices of Zhou. These practices still retained something of the ancient concern for virtue and conduct. Although the Tang had many examination categories, two endured longest: Illuminating the Classics and Presented Scholars (jinshi). Candidates in the Presented Scholars category studied tonal patterns and rhyme without grounding themselves in classical learning; those in Illuminating the Classics demonstrated skill in supplying concealed passages and recitation without investigating meaning and principle. Virtue and conduct were no longer considered.

Early in the Song, these two categories remained in use together. Only with Wang Anshi were the various categories all abolished. Scholars were ordered each to declare one classic as their specialization—the Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites of Zhou, or Record of Rites—together with the Analects and Mencius. Each examination comprised four sessions: essays on classical meaning probed their learning, while discourses and policy essays tested their judgment and deliberation. He further declared: “The aim is to unify moral understanding and bring customs into accord.”

The methods of the Han, Tang, and Song all succeeded in finding capable men. Yet, considered in their essentials, the system introduced through reforms during the Song had features that ought not to be discarded. The Han system approached antiquity, but would be difficult to implement today. The Tang system prized literary accomplishment, but its substance was not fully developed [?]. The Song replaced tonal composition with reasoned discussion and written answers on textual details with exposition of the broader meaning. Among scholars who answered policy questions and secured examination success, there might thus be some who recited the teachings left by the sages and worthies and glimpsed their underlying intentions. This is what makes that method worth adopting. Although it cannot yet be compared with the threefold instruction of the Zhou at its height, among the systems of later ages it was the better one.

Where did the method of evaluating officials begin? Since the practice of requiring reports and openly testing performance appears in the court of Shun, the system of assessing accomplishments has a distant origin. Yet none…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
備於周也周禮太宰掌計羣吏之治終歲
之間旬有日成月有月要歲有歲會百官
各正其治受其會聽其致事而詔其廢置
三歲則大計而誅賞之聽之以六計馭之
以八柄而淑慝于是乎分焉其法精且密
矣故當時在位罔非吉士而咸和永清之
化有由然也自是以降漢以六條按郡國
曰強豪踰制曰背公向私曰不恤疑獄曰
選署不平曰恃勢請託曰違公損下所謂
===
六條也唐以九等課百司敘之以四善曰
德義有聞曰清謹名著曰公平可稱曰恪
勤匪懈而緯之以二十七最自近侍至於
鎮防一最四善爲上上一最三善爲上中
一最二善爲上下無最而有二善爲中上
無最而有一善爲中中職事粗理善最不
聞爲中下愛憎任情處斷乖理爲下上背
公向私職務廢缺爲下中居官諂詐貪得
有狀爲下下所謂九等也宋以七事考轉
punctuated:
備於周也。《周禮》，太宰掌計羣吏之治。終歲之間，旬有日成，月有月要，歲有歲會。百官各正其治，受其會，聽其致事，而詔其廢置。三歲則大計而誅賞之，聽之以六計，馭之以八柄，而淑慝于是乎分焉。其法精且密矣，故當時在位罔非吉士，而咸和永清之化有由然也。
自是以降，漢以六條按郡國：曰強豪踰制，曰背公向私，曰不恤疑獄，曰選署不平，曰恃勢請託，曰違公損下，所謂六條也。唐以九等課百司，敘之以四善：曰德義有聞，曰清謹名著，曰公平可稱，曰恪勤匪懈。而緯之以二十七最，自近侍至於鎮防。一最四善爲上上，一最三善爲上中，一最二善爲上下，無最而有二善爲中上，無最而有一善爲中中，職事粗理、善最不聞爲中下，愛憎任情、處斷乖理爲下上，背公向私、職務廢缺爲下中，居官諂詐、貪得有狀爲下下，所謂九等也。宋以七事考轉
translation_en:
…more fully developed than under the Zhou. According to the Rites of Zhou, the Grand Steward was responsible for evaluating the administration of all officials. Throughout the year, each ten-day period had its daily records of accomplishments, each month its monthly summaries, and each year its annual accounts. The officials each put their administration in order; the Grand Steward received their accounts, heard their reports on the conduct of affairs, and advised the ruler on their dismissal or retention. Every three years he conducted a comprehensive evaluation and imposed punishments or rewards. He judged them by the six criteria of assessment and controlled them through the eight prerogatives, thereby distinguishing the good from the wicked. These methods were precise and thorough. Thus, those holding office at the time were without exception worthy men; this explains how a transforming influence that brought universal harmony and enduring tranquillity came about.
Thereafter, the Han inspected commanderies and kingdoms according to six articles: powerful local magnates overstepping prescribed limits; turning away from public duty toward private interests; failing to give due care to doubtful judicial cases; unfairness in selecting and appointing officials; relying on influence to solicit favors; and violating the public interest to the detriment of those below. These were the so-called six articles. The Tang evaluated the various offices according to nine grades, ranking officials by four virtues: a reputation for virtue and righteousness; a distinguished name for integrity and circumspection; praiseworthy fairness and impartiality; and conscientious diligence without slackening. These were combined with twenty-seven standards of outstanding performance, covering duties from close attendance upon the ruler to garrison defense. One outstanding performance and four virtues earned the upper grade of the upper class; one outstanding performance and three virtues, the middle grade of the upper class; one outstanding performance and two virtues, the lower grade of the upper class. No outstanding performance but two virtues earned the upper grade of the middle class; no outstanding performance but one virtue, the middle grade of the middle class. Adequate management of official duties, without any recognized virtue or outstanding performance, earned the lower grade of the middle class. Allowing personal likes and dislikes free rein and making unreasonable decisions earned the upper grade of the lower class. Turning away from public duty toward private interests and leaving official duties neglected or unfulfilled earned the middle grade of the lower class. Flattery and deceit in office, with documented instances of acquisitive greed, earned the lower grade of the lower class. These were the so-called nine grades. The Song used seven matters to evaluate transport …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
運提舉等官曰舉官曰勸農桑曰招流亡
曰興利除害曰案察部吏贓罪曰平反獄
訟曰覺察盜賊所謂七事也以九事考校
縣令曰斷獄平允曰賦稅不擾曰差徭均
曰盜賊屏曰勸農曰恤孤寡曰修水利曰
戶口增衍曰整治簿書所謂九事也漢唐
宋之法皆能致治然漢制主於按劾近於
刻峭宋制詳於文法失之重複唐則善以
著其德行最以著其才術以善與最相爲
===
乘除分爲九等上者加階其次進祿其下
奪祿又其下解任詳於善而略於最此其
法之可取也雖非成周大計之治而後世
之制則爲彼善矣洪惟我
朝損益前代之制著立一定之法其取士也
旣羣之學校以養之矣乃董之以師儒督
之以憲臣而就試之制則倣宋儒所謂貢
舉私議者三年大比登俊於鄉卽鄉大夫
之興禮也上之禮闈以俟
punctuated:
運、提舉等官，曰舉官，曰勸農桑，曰招流亡，曰興利除害，曰案察部吏贓罪，曰平反獄訟，曰覺察盜賊，所謂七事也。以九事考校縣令，曰斷獄平允，曰賦稅不擾，曰差徭均，曰盜賊屏，曰勸農，曰恤孤寡，曰修水利，曰戶口增衍，曰整治簿書，所謂九事也。漢、唐、宋之法皆能致治，然漢制主於按劾，近於刻峭；宋制詳於文法，失之重複；唐則善以著其德行，最以著其才術，以善與最相爲乘除，分爲九等。上者加階，其次進祿，其下奪祿，又其下解任。詳於善而略於最，此其法之可取也。雖非成周大計之治，而後世之制則爲彼善矣。
洪惟我朝損益前代之制，著立一定之法。其取士也，旣羣之學校以養之矣，乃董之以師儒，督之以憲臣，而就試之制則倣宋儒所謂《貢舉私議》者。三年大比，登俊於鄉，卽鄉大夫之興禮也。上之禮闈，以俟
translation_en:
…Transport Commissioners, Superintendents, and other officials: recommending men for office; encouraging agriculture and sericulture; bringing back displaced people; promoting benefits and eliminating harms; investigating corruption among subordinate officials; reviewing and rectifying judicial cases; and detecting bandits and thieves. These were the so-called seven matters. Nine matters were used to evaluate District Magistrates: fairness in deciding judicial cases; collecting taxes without harassing the people; equitable allocation of labor service; suppression of bandits and thieves; encouragement of agriculture; relief for orphans and widows; maintenance of waterworks; growth in the number of households and population; and orderly management of registers and documents. These were the so-called nine matters.
The methods of the Han, Tang, and Song could all produce good government. Yet the Han system emphasized investigation and impeachment, verging on excessive severity; the Song system elaborated documentary rules, falling into needless repetition. Under the Tang, assessments of “goodness” disclosed officials’ moral conduct, while assessments of “excellence” disclosed their abilities and administrative skills. Goodness and excellence were weighed together, with merits and shortcomings offset against one another, to distinguish nine grades. Those in the highest grades received advancement in rank; those next below received increased stipends; those lower down lost stipends; and those still lower were dismissed from office. Its detailed treatment of goodness and comparatively brief treatment of excellence were what made this method worthy of adoption. Although it did not constitute the government of the comprehensive assessment system of the Zhou at its height, among the institutions of later ages it was comparatively good.
We reverently reflect that our dynasty has modified the institutions of preceding ages and established a fixed body of regulations. In selecting men for office, it first gathers them in schools to nurture them, then places them under the guidance of scholarly instructors and the supervision of censorial officials. Its examination system follows what a Song Confucian scholar called Private Proposals on Recruitment by Recommendation and Examination (Gongju siyi). Every three years, a great assessment raises up outstanding men through the Provincial Examination: this is precisely the rite by which the Zhou District Grand Masters advanced worthy men. They are then sent on to the examination precincts of the Ministry of Rites to await…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
廷對卽大司馬之進士也此蓋本虞周之意
而兼漢唐宋之美一代士類之進濟濟乎
明揚賓興之盛矣其課吏也旣分之職事
以責之矣乃糾之以監司統之以臺省而
考語所書則取唐人所爲等其善最者九
年通考第其升降卽虞廷之考績也三載
述事大明黜陟卽周官之大計也此蓋監
虞周之制而集漢唐宋之成一代吏治之
飭翼翼乎慶賞刑威之嚴矣二百年于茲
===
名卿碩輔于是乎出內輯外寧于是乎效
孰非選舉考課之美而得人維治之功哉
是宜萬世遵行永遠無弊固無以議爲者
然而論者猶以科舉之文不適實用考課
之法未免失眞愚則以爲非法之弊也有
治人無治法存乎其人焉耳夫所善於選
舉者爲其無失人也然用法之精在人而
不在法是非邪正吾懸鑑以照之則雖用
今之法而自可以得人不必其合於古否
punctuated:
廷對，卽大司馬之進士也。此蓋本虞周之意，而兼漢唐宋之美，一代士類之進，濟濟乎明揚賓興之盛矣。其課吏也，旣分之職事以責之矣，乃糾之以監司，統之以臺省，而考語所書，則取唐人所爲等其善最者。九年通考，第其升降，卽虞廷之考績也；三載述事，大明黜陟，卽周官之大計也。此蓋監虞周之制，而集漢唐宋之成，一代吏治之飭，翼翼乎慶賞刑威之嚴矣。二百年于茲，名卿碩輔于是乎出，內輯外寧于是乎效，孰非選舉考課之美，而得人維治之功哉？是宜萬世遵行，永遠無弊，固無以議爲者。
然而論者猶以科舉之文不適實用，考課之法未免失眞。愚則以爲非法之弊也，有治人，無治法，存乎其人焉耳。夫所善於選舉者，爲其無失人也。然用法之精，在人而不在法。是非邪正，吾懸鑑以照之，則雖用今之法，而自可以得人，不必其合於古否
translation_en:
…to answer questions at court: this corresponds to the Grand Minister of War’s advancement of worthy men. This system takes its underlying purpose from Yu and Zhou while incorporating the strengths of Han, Tang, and Song. In the advancement of scholars under our dynasty, how splendid is the multitude of worthy men publicly recognized and recommended with the honors accorded to guests! In evaluating officials, duties are first apportioned to establish their responsibilities; surveillance officials then scrutinize them, and the Censorate and central administration oversee them. The written assessments adopt the Tang practice of grading officials according to their virtues and outstanding achievements. A comprehensive evaluation every nine years determines promotion and demotion: this corresponds to performance evaluation at the court of Yu. Reporting achievements every three years and clearly determining dismissal and advancement corresponds to the grand evaluation prescribed in the Offices of Zhou. This system takes the institutions of Yu and Zhou as its model and brings together the accomplishments of Han, Tang, and Song. In regulating official administration under our dynasty, how solemn and exacting are its rewards and punishments! For two hundred years now, eminent ministers and great counselors have emerged through this system, and internal harmony and external peace have resulted from it. Are these not all the benefits of selection and performance evaluation, and the achievements of securing worthy men to sustain good government? These institutions ought therefore to be followed for ten thousand generations, forever free of defects; there would indeed seem to be nothing to criticize.
Yet critics still hold that examination writing is unsuited to practical use and that methods of evaluating officials do not always reflect their true performance. In my humble view, these are not defects in the institutions. There are men who bring about good government, but no methods that bring it about of themselves: everything depends on the people involved. What we value in selection is that it overlooks no worthy person. Yet precision in applying its methods depends on people, not on the methods themselves. If we hang up a mirror to illuminate right and wrong, the corrupt and the upright, then even with today’s methods we can secure worthy men, without needing to consider whether they accord with antiquity…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
也所善於考課者爲其無失事也然用法
之核在人而不在法進退黜陟吾持衡以
平之則雖用今之法而亦可以課吏不必
其合於古否也何也科目不足以得士則
將舍此而鄉舉里選乎風氣日流奸僞日
甚即今試法之嚴猶恐僥濫厠迹爲清議
訾使壹用辟召是開弊竇而長倖梯也夫
科目之累人非科目之累也學術之不正
使之也今之應舉者有不誦法聖賢者乎
===
窮經而致用世未嘗之人也然務勦說而
鮮自得軼師傳而詭時好者亦時有之宜
乎識者有虛名亡實之憂也雖然亦明以
辨之而已根理之學不飾而妍枝葉之辭
雖工亦厭詖淫邪遁者必斥勿長浮薄之
風典雅朴茂者必錄冀收沉實之用如是
其於人材真僞亦庶幾乎拔十得五矣有
不足爲世道之助乎考課慮其失真則將
如虞廷三考而後黜陟耶虐政害民朝弗
punctuated: 也。所善於考課者，爲其無失事也。然用法之核，在人而不在法。進退黜陟，吾持衡以平之，則雖用今之法，而亦可以課吏，不必其合於古否也。何也？科目不足以得士，則將舍此而鄉舉里選乎？風氣日流，奸僞日甚，即今試法之嚴，猶恐僥濫厠迹，爲清議訾；使壹用辟召，是開弊竇而長倖梯也。夫科目之累人，非科目之累也，學術之不正使之也。今之應舉者，有不誦法聖賢者乎？窮經而致用，世未嘗之人也。然務勦說而鮮自得，軼師傳而詭時好者，亦時有之。宜乎識者有虛名亡實之憂也。雖然，亦明以辨之而已。根理之學，不飾而妍；枝葉之辭，雖工亦厭。詖淫邪遁者必斥，勿長浮薄之風；典雅朴茂者必錄，冀收沉實之用。如是，其於人材真僞，亦庶幾乎拔十得五矣。有不足爲世道之助乎？考課慮其失真，則將如虞廷三考而後黜陟耶？虐政害民，朝弗
translation_en:
…so it is. What is commendable in performance evaluations is that no duty is neglected. Yet rigor in applying the rules depends on the person, not on the rules. If we hold the scales impartially when advancing or retiring, dismissing or promoting officials, then even the present rules suffice to evaluate them; it need not matter whether those rules accord with antiquity. Why is this? If examination categories are insufficient to obtain worthy scholars, are we to abandon them for nomination by townships and selection by villages? Customs deteriorate daily, and deceit and imposture grow ever worse. Even with the present examination rules so strict, we still fear that undeserving men may slip into the ranks through luck or indiscriminate admission, inviting censure from informed public opinion. To rely exclusively on recruitment by invitation would open avenues for abuse and provide a ladder for advancement through mere good fortune. When examinations compromise men, the fault does not lie in the examinations: it is their unsound learning that causes this.

Among those now presenting themselves for examination, is there anyone who does not recite the teachings of the sages and worthies and take them as models? The world has never lacked people who thoroughly study the classics and put their learning to practical use [?]. Yet there are also those who devote themselves to appropriating others’ explanations and gain little understanding of their own, or who depart from their teachers’ transmission and devise strange arguments to suit contemporary tastes. No wonder discerning people worry about empty reputation without substance. Nevertheless, all that is needed is clear discernment. Learning rooted in principle is beautiful without ornament; merely superficial language is tiresome even when skillfully composed. Those whose words are biased, extravagant, deviant, or evasive must be rejected, lest a frivolous and shallow disposition be encouraged. Those whose writing is refined, correct, plain, and substantial must be selected, in the hope of securing the services of steady and substantial men. In this way, in distinguishing genuine talent from counterfeit, we might come close to finding five worthy men among every ten selected. Would this not help improve the moral condition of the age?

If we fear that performance evaluations fail to reflect the truth, must we follow the court of Shun and wait for three evaluations before dismissing or promoting officials? Oppressive government harms the people; from morning there is not…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
及夕即今法網之密猶恐奇袤逸罰爲治
體累使更用疏闊是滋官邪而重民患也
夫考課之病治非考課之病也稱量之弗
協使之也今之服官者有不顧畏名義者
乎爲善而務實世未嘗乏人也然背公義
而植私交飾僞價而徼市利者亦或有之
宜乎識者有任法失人之懼也雖然亦公
以持之而已賢者必進不以私抑不肖者
必退不以情免悃愊無華者毋以悶悶而
===
遺其賢奔競爲悅者毋以矯矯而没其不
肖如是其於人材之進退亦庶幾乎十不
失一矣有不足爲治典之光乎抑猶未也
今之選擧旣竭其明矣而執事猶遺賢是
懼惓惓之誠是也愚則以方今之士景附響
從視古之鄕擧里選不啻盛矣合網羅而
囊括之一藝一能無不自效而豈遺賢之
患雖然有一說焉取士以試應試以文而
賢能所儲初不在是也必也明敎化乎今
punctuated:
及夕。即今法網之密，猶恐奇袤逸罰，爲治體累；使更用疏闊，是滋官邪而重民患也。夫考課之病治，非考課之病也，稱量之弗協使之也。今之服官者，有不顧畏名義者乎？爲善而務實，世未嘗乏人也。然背公義而植私交，飾僞價而徼市利者，亦或有之。宜乎識者有任法失人之懼也。雖然，亦公以持之而已。賢者必進，不以私抑；不肖者必退，不以情免。悃愊無華者，毋以悶悶而遺其賢；奔競爲悅者，毋以矯矯而没其不肖。如是，其於人材之進退，亦庶幾乎十不失一矣。有不足爲治典之光乎？

抑猶未也。今之選擧，旣竭其明矣，而執事猶遺賢是懼，惓惓之誠是也。愚則以方今之士景附響從，視古之鄕擧里選，不啻盛矣。合網羅而囊括之，一藝一能，無不自效，而豈遺賢之患？雖然，有一說焉：取士以試，應試以文，而賢能所儲，初不在是也。必也明敎化乎！今
translation_en:
…until evening. Even with the legal net as tightly woven as it is today, there is still fear that aberrant wrongdoing [?] will escape punishment and burden the administration. If still looser measures were adopted, this would foster official misconduct and aggravate the people's suffering. When performance evaluations harm government, the fault does not lie in evaluation itself: it arises from an improper weighing of merit. Among those holding office today, are there any who pay no heed to reputation and moral obligation? The world has never lacked people who do good and attend to substantive achievements. Yet there are also some who turn their backs on public duty to cultivate private connections, inflate their worth through false appearances, and seek advantages as though bargaining in a market. It is fitting that discerning men should fear that reliance on regulations may lead to mistakes in judging people. Nevertheless, all that is needed is to administer them impartially. The worthy must be promoted, never held back for private reasons; the unworthy must be dismissed, never spared out of personal affection. Those who are sincere and unadorned must not have their worth overlooked because they seem dull; those who scramble for advancement and seek to please must not have their unworthiness concealed by an imposing manner. If this is done, promotions and dismissals might well proceed without a single error in ten. Would this not bring distinction to the institutions of government?

Yet this is still not enough. In selecting men for office today, you have already exercised your discernment to the utmost; nevertheless, you who conduct this work still fear overlooking worthy men. This reveals your earnest sincerity. In my humble view, the scholars of our day flock to the examinations as shadows follow forms and echoes follow sounds, in numbers more than rivaling the ancient system of recommendation by districts and selection by villages. They should all be gathered in and embraced, so that anyone possessing even one skill or ability can offer his service. What fear would there then be of overlooking worthy men? Nevertheless, there is another point to make: scholars are selected through examinations, and they take these examinations by composing essays, but virtue and ability do not fundamentally reside in such writing. Surely moral instruction must be made clear! Now…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
夫樹棘者得刺樹果者得實養之貴以豫
也周官選舉之法敎以德行使民興賢敎
以道藝使民興能興賢則出使長之興能
則入使治之是以民無弗服而事無弗理
眞才可得而用也今也師儒之所敎憲臣
之所督非不曰德行道藝也然誘之以利
祿之途敎之以文字之學所重固有在矣
誘之使來而復禁其趨敎之已成而顧違
其用是所望非所樹也必不然矣竊以爲
===
養士者必重師儒之選而申本實之敎課
之以經義則校其躬行而不徒采其華課
之以世務必求其實用而不徒騰其說德
行道藝彬彬可睹如胡瑗所謂經義治事
者然後學官書其績憲臣攷其成雖科目
所舉專以其文而行藝之脩則旣備矣異
日之所使卽今日之所敎尚何人材之不
可用而遺賢是虞乎是故科舉莫先於明
敎化也今之考課旣極其公矣而執事猶
punctuated:
夫樹棘者得刺，樹果者得實，養之貴以豫也。《周官》選舉之法，敎以德行，使民興賢；敎以道藝，使民興能。興賢則出使長之，興能則入使治之。是以民無弗服，而事無弗理，眞才可得而用也。今也，師儒之所敎，憲臣之所督，非不曰德行道藝也。然誘之以利祿之途，敎之以文字之學，所重固有在矣。誘之使來，而復禁其趨；敎之已成，而顧違其用，是所望非所樹也，必不然矣。

竊以爲，養士者必重師儒之選，而申本實之敎。課之以經義，則校其躬行，而不徒采其華；課之以世務，必求其實用，而不徒騰其說。德行道藝，彬彬可睹，如胡瑗所謂經義治事者。然後學官書其績，憲臣攷其成。雖科目所舉專以其文，而行藝之脩則旣備矣。異日之所使，卽今日之所敎，尚何人材之不可用，而遺賢是虞乎？是故科舉莫先於明敎化也。今之考課旣極其公矣，而執事猶
translation_en:
…Those who plant thorns obtain prickles; those who plant fruit trees obtain fruit. In nurturing, what matters is preparing beforehand. Under the system of selection and recommendation in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan), people were taught virtue and conduct, so that they would recommend the worthy; they were taught the Way and practical arts, so that they would recommend the capable. Those recommended for worthiness were sent out to lead the people; those recommended for ability were brought in to administer affairs. Thus none among the people failed to submit, and no affairs went unregulated: genuine talent could be found and employed. Today, what scholarly teachers teach and censorial officials oversee is likewise said to be virtue, conduct, the Way, and practical arts. Yet students are enticed by the prospect of profit and official emoluments and instructed in literary composition: plainly, this is where the emphasis lies.
