經筵之御，崇儒之心也。將經筵之一御，而謂足以盡崇儒之實也，可乎？大學之臨，重道之心也。將大學之一臨，而謂足以盡重道之實也，可乎？故方其御講之時，蓋聞乎聖人之言矣，義理之感發，必有勃然而聽之忘倦者。吾不知退而優游泮渙之時，猶能尋而繹之，以求其精義之歸乎？抑師保之不臨，而惟其心之所好，以馳騖於他技已也？方其
translation_en:
…among those gathered around the school gate to listen. I can only bow my head and extol these achievements; words cannot exhaust their praise. As for contributing to deliberation and reflection, I have scarcely any notion how to do so. Yet I have heard of a man who, knowing only the multiplication table, dared seek reception as a guest in Qi; and of another who found celery sweet and wished to offer it to his ruler, unaware of the exquisite foods already available to him. Since your discerning question touches upon this matter, how could I dare withhold the one small insight of my foolish understanding? Thus, those who demand substance do not settle for mere reputation, and bringing something to a fine conclusion depends upon setting its beginning right. If there have been actions like those of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, yet their substantial achievements remain unseen; if beginnings like theirs have been made, yet their full effects remain unrealized—can the gentleman be without concern? Let us speak, for now, of His Majesty’s learning today.
His attendance at the Classics Colloquium expresses his intention to honor Confucian scholars. But can one claim that a single attendance suffices to fulfill that intention in substance? His visit to the Imperial University expresses his intention to esteem the Way. But can one claim that a single visit suffices to fulfill that intention in substance? When he attends a lecture, he hears the words of the sages; stirred by their moral principles, he must surely experience a surge of inspiration and listen without weariness. I do not know whether, after withdrawing into leisure and relaxation, he still pursues and unfolds what he has heard, seeking the ultimate purport of its subtle principles. Or, when his preceptors and guardians are absent, does he merely follow his heart’s preferences and pursue other skills? Just when he…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
幸學之際蓋游於聖人之門矣道德之儀刑必
有奮然而從之末由者吾不知退而燕居
獨處之際猶能常目在之以永其寤寐之
思乎抑宮牆之旣遠而惟其身之所接以
依違乎近習已也夫一暴十寒非所以進
於善也理欲交戰非所以純其心也况荒
寧是懼則二帝三王之成憲具昭存省有
常則
二祖列聖之家敎如在是故始之以務學之勤
===
而遜志時敏則寒暑不輟如
憲皇可也廣之以虛受之益而樂善兼容則箴
規不忌如
孝皇可也由是而存心以端其本則幾微必審
也由是而省躬以防其欲則舉動必愼也
經書之表章者不惟玩其議論而深思其
心法之精倫書之編輯者不惟考其典故
而力求其身體之實是故他技雖足以投
吾好也而此心常若保傅之在前近習雖
punctuated: 幸學之際，蓋游於聖人之門矣。道德之儀刑，必有奮然而從之末由者。吾不知退而燕居獨處之際，猶能常目在之，以永其寤寐之思乎？抑宮牆之旣遠，而惟其身之所接，以依違乎近習已也？夫一暴十寒，非所以進於善也；理欲交戰，非所以純其心也。况荒寧是懼，則二帝三王之成憲具昭；存省有常，則二祖列聖之家敎如在。是故始之以務學之勤，而遜志時敏，則寒暑不輟，如憲皇可也；廣之以虛受之益，而樂善兼容，則箴規不忌，如孝皇可也。由是而存心以端其本，則幾微必審也；由是而省躬以防其欲，則舉動必愼也。經書之表章者，不惟玩其議論，而深思其心法之精；倫書之編輯者，不惟考其典故，而力求其身體之實。是故他技雖足以投吾好也，而此心常若保傅之在前；近習雖
translation_en:
…when visiting the imperial academy, you have indeed entered the gate of the sages. Confronted with their exemplary moral virtue, you must surely have felt stirred to emulate them, yet found no way to do so. I do not know whether, after withdrawing to dwell quietly alone, you can still keep them constantly before your eyes and sustain your thoughts of them waking and sleeping. Or, once far from the academy’s walls, do you merely accommodate yourself to familiar attendants, guided by those with whom you associate?

One day of warmth followed by ten days of cold is no way to advance in goodness; contention between principle and desire is no way to make the heart pure. Moreover, if you fear idle ease, the established precedents of the Two Emperors and Three Kings stand fully revealed; if you constantly preserve and examine your heart, the family teachings of the Two Founding Emperors and the succession of sage rulers remain as though present before you. Thus, begin with diligence in learning: humble your mind and apply yourself assiduously, continuing through cold and heat without interruption, as Emperor Xian did. Broaden this through the benefits of receptive humility: delight in goodness and embrace diverse counsel, taking no offense at admonition, as Emperor Xiao did.

By thus preserving the heart to rectify its foundation, you will surely scrutinize the subtlest stirrings of thought; by thus examining yourself to guard against desire, you will surely exercise care in every action. As for the canonical writings you honor and promote, do more than ponder their arguments: reflect deeply upon the refinement of their methods for cultivating the heart. As for the books on human relationships that have been compiled, do more than investigate their precedents: strive earnestly to put their teachings into practice yourself. Thus, although other pursuits may appeal to my tastes, my heart will always feel as though its guardians and tutors stood before it; although familiar attendants…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
足以順吾旨也而此心常若聖賢之相對
崇儒而必求真儒則講論切而理可明矣
重道而不惑於非道則趨向一而心可端
矣理明而是非之極自定心端而邪正之
辨自嚴是非之極定於內而凡進言之臣
是者行之非者置之而確乎其不易否則
漫然不加可否雖無拒諫之非而亦未見
有從諫之實也邪正之辨嚴於外而凡效
用之臣正者任之邪者去之而斷乎其無
===
疑否則混然無所決擇雖無遺賢之嘆而
亦未見得任賢之實也嗚呼人君之德存
心務學其大端也君德之用任賢納諫其
大致也從事於四者之間而朝夕匪懈何
患乎德之不盛而業之不廣也哉抑愚生
又有進焉守
祖宗之心法而紹堯舜禹湯文武之傳以無負
於上天付託之意者吾
君之事也廣論思之忠益而繼皐陶伊傅周召
punctuated:
足以順吾旨也，而此心常若聖賢之相對。崇儒而必求真儒，則講論切而理可明矣；重道而不惑於非道，則趨向一而心可端矣。理明而是非之極自定，心端而邪正之辨自嚴。是非之極定於內，而凡進言之臣，是者行之，非者置之，而確乎其不易；否則漫然不加可否，雖無拒諫之非，而亦未見有從諫之實也。邪正之辨嚴於外，而凡效用之臣，正者任之，邪者去之，而斷乎其無疑；否則混然無所決擇，雖無遺賢之嘆，而亦未見得任賢之實也。
嗚呼！人君之德，存心務學，其大端也；君德之用，任賢納諫，其大致也。從事於四者之間，而朝夕匪懈，何患乎德之不盛而業之不廣也哉？抑愚生又有進焉：守祖宗之心法，而紹堯舜禹湯文武之傳，以無負於上天付託之意者，吾君之事也；廣論思之忠益，而繼皐陶伊傅周召
translation_en:
…may readily comply with my wishes, yet my mind remains as though confronting the sages and worthies. If one honors Confucian scholars and insists on seeking true scholars, their discussions will be pertinent and principle can become clear. If one esteems the Way and is not misled by what is contrary to it, one’s purpose will be unified and one’s mind can be rectified. When principle is clear, the standard of right and wrong naturally becomes settled; when the mind is upright, the distinction between the crooked and the upright naturally becomes strict. With the standard of right and wrong settled within, one implements what is right in the proposals of ministers who offer counsel and sets aside what is wrong, remaining firm and unchanging in this. Otherwise, if one heedlessly makes no judgment of approval or disapproval, although one may not be guilty of rejecting remonstrance, neither is there any evidence of actually following it. With the distinction between the crooked and the upright rigorously applied in external affairs, one employs the upright among the ministers who offer their services and dismisses the crooked, acting decisively and without doubt. Otherwise, if one muddles along without making a definite choice, although there may be no lament that worthy men have been overlooked, neither is there any evidence of actually employing them.
Ah! Preserving the mind and diligently pursuing learning are the principal elements of a ruler’s virtue; employing the worthy and accepting remonstrance are the chief ways in which that virtue is put into practice. If one applies oneself to these four things, never slackening morning or evening, why worry that one’s virtue will not flourish or one’s achievements not expand? Yet this humble student has something further to offer: to preserve the ancestral methods of cultivating the mind and continue the tradition of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, so as not to fail the trust placed in him by Heaven above, is the task of our sovereign; to broaden the benefits of loyal deliberation and reflection, and to carry forward the achievements of Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
之績以無愧於儒者功用之全則諸臣之
責也是故有以玩人喪德玩物喪志敬勝
怠義勝欲之說進者是欲
上為文武也有以無敎逸欲無曠庶官不邇聲
色不殖貨利之說進者是欲
上為禹湯也有以罔遊于逸罔淫于樂任賢勿
貳去邪勿疑之說進者是欲
上為堯舜也夫欲致其君為堯舜禹湯文武者
忠之大者也其君聽而用之成其臣為皐
===
陶伊傅周召者聖之至者也然必臣止於
敬而後可以感其君之敬故曰惟大人為
能格其君心夫臣以敬格君而君又以敬
自格是所謂咸有一德也由是前後左右
罔非正人而出入起居罔有不欽則長夜
之屏不足箴千秋之鑑祗為贅耳如君心
未格而曰我善論思豈愚所敢信乎蠡管
之見若此惟執事可否之
第二問
punctuated:
之績，以無愧於儒者功用之全，則諸臣之責也。是故有以「玩人喪德，玩物喪志，敬勝怠，義勝欲」之說進者，是欲上為文武也；有以「無敎逸欲，無曠庶官，不邇聲色，不殖貨利」之說進者，是欲上為禹湯也；有以「罔遊于逸，罔淫于樂，任賢勿貳，去邪勿疑」之說進者，是欲上為堯舜也。夫欲致其君為堯舜禹湯文武者，忠之大者也；其君聽而用之，成其臣為皐陶伊傅周召者，聖之至者也。然必臣止於敬，而後可以感其君之敬。故曰：「惟大人為能格其君心。」夫臣以敬格君，而君又以敬自格，是所謂「咸有一德」也。由是前後左右罔非正人，而出入起居罔有不欽，則長夜之屏不足箴，千秋之鑑祗為贅耳。如君心未格，而曰「我善論思」，豈愚所敢信乎？蠡管之見若此，惟執事可否之。
第二問
translation_en:
…their achievements, so as to do justice to the full practical efficacy of Confucian learning: this is the responsibility of the ministers. Thus, those who submit the teachings, “Treating people as playthings destroys virtue; delighting in objects destroys resolve; reverence overcomes indolence; righteousness overcomes desire,” wish His Majesty to become like Wen and Wu. Those who submit the teachings, “Do not encourage ease and desire; leave none of the offices unfilled; do not draw near to alluring music and beauty; do not accumulate wealth and profit,” wish His Majesty to become like Yu and Tang. Those who submit the teachings, “Do not wander in idleness; do not indulge excessively in pleasure; appoint the worthy without wavering; remove the wicked without hesitation,” wish His Majesty to become like Yao and Shun. Wishing to make one’s ruler a Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, or Wu is loyalty at its greatest. For the ruler to listen and act upon such counsel, thereby enabling his ministers to become like Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, is sagehood at its utmost.
Yet ministers must first abide in reverence before they can awaken reverence in their ruler. Thus it is said, “Only a great man can rectify his ruler’s heart.” When ministers rectify their ruler through reverence, and the ruler likewise rectifies himself through reverence, this is what is meant by “all possessing one virtue.” Consequently, those before, behind, and on either side of him will all be upright men, and in going out and coming in, rising and resting, he will never lack reverence. Then the screen bearing the admonition against long nights of revelry would have nothing left to correct, and the Mirror for a Thousand Autumns would merely be superfluous. If the ruler’s heart remains unrectified, yet someone says, “I am skilled at deliberation and reflection,” how could I, in my ignorance, venture to believe him? Such are my narrow views, like measuring with a ladle or peering through a tube. I ask you, honored examiners, to judge their merits.
Second Question

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
黃雲繪
同考試官教諭伍批我
皇上好生之德與天地並中外臣工咸思祗承
德意躋斯世於仁壽之域子能悉心敷陳有欽若之意焉宜錄以獻
同考試官教諭鄭批我
皇上停刑肆赦與古帝王欽恤同心是篇得大意而闡揚之末復以持平責
文法吏其達於弼教之義者矣
考試官教授吳批以欽恤頌
聖德以平恕責有司皆確論也取之
===
考試官教授李批以仁義並言得明刑之㫖
帝王之治天下也德可以化民乎曰可然
從違順逆之異齊君子不容不正之以義
法可以齊民乎曰可然輕重出入之異致
君子不容不濟之以仁夫惟義有所當執
是法有不可廢者由是設刑而威不軌以
濟仁之不及則民見義而懷刑夫惟仁有
所當施是情有所可原者由是原情而宥
無辜以節義之大過則民蒙仁而懷德故
punctuated:
黃雲繪。

同考試官教諭伍批：我皇上好生之德與天地並，中外臣工咸思祗承德意，躋斯世於仁壽之域。子能悉心敷陳，有欽若之意焉，宜錄以獻。

同考試官教諭鄭批：我皇上停刑肆赦，與古帝王欽恤同心。是篇得大意而闡揚之，末復以持平責文法吏，其達於弼教之義者矣。

考試官教授吳批：以欽恤頌聖德，以平恕責有司，皆確論也，取之。

考試官教授李批：以仁義並言，得明刑之㫖。

帝王之治天下也，德可以化民乎？曰：可。然從違順逆之異齊，君子不容不正之以義。法可以齊民乎？曰：可。然輕重出入之異致，君子不容不濟之以仁。夫惟義有所當執，是法有不可廢者。由是設刑而威不軌，以濟仁之不及，則民見義而懷刑。夫惟仁有所當施，是情有所可原者。由是原情而宥無辜，以節義之大過，則民蒙仁而懷德。故
translation_en:
Huang Yunhui.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: “Our Emperor’s virtue of cherishing life equals that of Heaven and Earth. Officials at court and throughout the realm all seek reverently to carry out his benevolent intentions and bring this age into a realm of humaneness and longevity. You have expounded the matter with care and thoroughness, showing an intention reverently to comply. This deserves to be transcribed and presented to the throne.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “In suspending punishments and granting pardons, our Emperor shares the ancient emperors’ and kings’ concern for reverence and compassion in punishment. This essay grasps and elucidates the central meaning. At its close, it further demands impartiality of officials who administer the written law. Its author understands the principle that punishment assists moral instruction.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: “It praises the sage sovereign’s virtue for his reverence and compassion in punishment and demands fairness and forbearance of the responsible officials. These are all sound arguments. Accept it.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: “By discussing humaneness and righteousness together, it captures the purpose of making punishments clear.”

When emperors and kings govern all under Heaven, can virtue transform the people? The answer is yes. Yet, given the differences between compliance and disobedience, obedience and rebellion [?], the gentleman cannot but rectify them through righteousness. Can law bring the people into order? The answer is yes. Yet, given the differing outcomes of heavier and lighter penalties, and of imposing or remitting punishment, the gentleman cannot but temper it with humaneness. Precisely because righteousness includes principles that must be upheld, there are laws that cannot be abolished. Thus punishments are established to deter the lawless and make good what humaneness alone cannot accomplish; the people then perceive righteousness and hold punishments in mind. Precisely because humaneness has occasions on which it must be exercised, there are circumstances that warrant leniency. Thus circumstances are considered and the innocent pardoned, restraining excessive rigor in righteousness; the people then receive humaneness and cherish virtue. Therefore…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
仁可過也義不可過也書曰眚災肆赦又
曰罪疑惟輕蓋聖人之心惟恐殺一不辜
以傷天地之和也嗚呼用刑豈聖人所獲
已也哉知乎此則我
聖祖欽恤之仁與
皇上好生之德所以保合太和以仁壽斯世者
真同符于唐虞三代正中外臣工所宜惟
明惟允將奉
德意以無負於
===
===
熈時者也請因明問而敬陳之昔者聖人之畫
卦也於震下離上而噬嗑名焉象曰雷電
噬嗑先王以明罰勅法此聖人以法輔治
之義也於離下艮上爲賁象曰山下有火
賁君子以明庶政無敢折獄此聖人尚德
緩刑之仁也然於赦過宥罪則象諸解議
獄緩死則象諸中孚焉其至誠惻怛之心
欽恤哀矜之念可槩見矣是故舜以玄德
帝於虞有士師之命矣然欽哉惟恤而天
punctuated:
仁可過也，義不可過也。《書》曰：「眚災肆赦。」又曰：「罪疑惟輕。」蓋聖人之心，惟恐殺一不辜，以傷天地之和也。嗚呼！用刑豈聖人所獲已也哉？知乎此，則我聖祖欽恤之仁與皇上好生之德，所以保合太和，以仁壽斯世者，真同符于唐虞三代，正中外臣工所宜惟明惟允，將奉德意，以無負於熈時者也。請因明問而敬陳之。
昔者聖人之畫卦也，於震下離上而噬嗑名焉。《象》曰：「雷電，噬嗑；先王以明罰勅法。」此聖人以法輔治之義也。於離下艮上爲賁，《象》曰：「山下有火，賁；君子以明庶政，無敢折獄。」此聖人尚德緩刑之仁也。然於赦過宥罪，則象諸解；議獄緩死，則象諸中孚焉。其至誠惻怛之心，欽恤哀矜之念，可槩見矣。是故舜以玄德帝於虞，有士師之命矣。然「欽哉惟恤」，而天
translation_en:
…benevolence may go too far, but righteousness must not. The Book of Documents says, “Pardon inadvertent faults and misfortunes.” It also says, “When guilt is doubtful, impose the lighter penalty.” The sage’s heart fears above all that putting even one innocent person to death might injure the harmony of Heaven and Earth. Alas! Could the sage ever resort to punishment except from necessity? Understanding this, we recognize that the reverent concern and benevolence of our Sagely Ancestor, together with His Majesty’s life-loving virtue, preserve supreme harmony and bring benevolence and longevity to this age. These truly accord with the rule of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. It therefore falls to officials at court and in the provinces to act with discernment and fairness, carrying out the imperial benevolent intentions so as not to fail this flourishing age. Allow me respectfully to set this forth in response to your illuminating question.
When the sage anciently drew the hexagrams, he placed Zhen below and Li above and named the resulting hexagram Shihe, “Biting Through.” The Commentary on the Images says, “Thunder and lightning: Biting Through. The former kings thereby made penalties clear and put the laws in order.” This expresses the sage’s righteousness in using law to support government. With Li below and Gen above, the hexagram is Bi, “Adornment.” The Commentary on the Images says, “Fire below the mountain: Adornment. The gentleman thereby illuminates the various affairs of government, but does not venture to decide criminal cases.” This expresses the sage’s benevolence in honoring virtue and tempering punishment. Pardoning faults and forgiving crimes are modeled on Jie, “Release”; deliberating on criminal cases and delaying executions are modeled on Zhongfu, “Inner Sincerity.” Here we may broadly discern his utterly sincere and compassionate heart, his reverent concern and pity.
Thus Shun, through his profound virtue, ruled as emperor in Yu and issued a charge to the Judge. Yet he admonished, “Be reverent! Show compassion!” and all under Heaven…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
下咸服恩何渥耶禹以台德王於夏有常
刑之制矣然下車泣罪而兆民允懷仁何
溥耶成康業承于文武法備於周官則有
大司寇以掌邦禁以兩造禁民訟以兩劑
禁民獄及大司徒所掌八刑以糾萬民亦
旣詳且密矣然猶懼愚民之陷於罪也于
是詳之以五聽訊之以三刺原之以三赦
三宥而愼獄敬刑之訓藹然忠厚之家法
焉其後百姓免於刑戮興於禮義而囹圄
===
空虛者孰非仁心仁政之所培植也哉夫
四君者好生之德旣洽於敕法之先而不
忍之心每周於得情之後何曾輕議一辟
以損乎惻隱之仁此太和元氣在虞夏成
周宇宙間者信不誣矣周澤旣衰法令滋
起申韓馳騁於戰國斯高睚眦於嬴秦誹
謗者族誅偶語者棄市刑威熾而忠恕薄
無足論者嗣漢而下高帝約法三章文帝
詔除肉刑非不足以聯屬人心稱漢令主
punctuated:
下咸服，恩何渥耶！禹以台德王於夏，有常刑之制矣，然下車泣罪，而兆民允懷，仁何溥耶！成康業承于文武，法備於周官，則有大司寇以掌邦禁，以兩造禁民訟，以兩劑禁民獄；及大司徒所掌八刑，以糾萬民，亦旣詳且密矣。然猶懼愚民之陷於罪也，于是詳之以五聽，訊之以三刺，原之以三赦三宥，而愼獄敬刑之訓，藹然忠厚之家法焉。其後百姓免於刑戮，興於禮義，而囹圄空虛者，孰非仁心仁政之所培植也哉！夫四君者，好生之德旣洽於敕法之先，而不忍之心每周於得情之後，何曾輕議一辟，以損乎惻隱之仁？此太和元氣在虞夏成周宇宙間者，信不誣矣。
周澤旣衰，法令滋起，申韓馳騁於戰國，斯高睚眦於嬴秦。誹謗者族誅，偶語者棄市，刑威熾而忠恕薄，無足論者。嗣漢而下，高帝約法三章，文帝詔除肉刑，非不足以聯屬人心，稱漢令主
translation_en:
…all under Heaven submitted: how abundant was his grace! Yu, through his own virtue, ruled as king over Xia and established regular punishments. Yet he descended from his carriage and wept over offenders, and the myriad people truly cherished him: how far-reaching was his benevolence! Kings Cheng and Kang inherited the enterprise of Kings Wen and Wu, and their laws were fully set forth in the Offices of Zhou. The Minister of Justice administered the realm’s prohibitions, restraining civil litigation by requiring the appearance of both parties, and criminal litigation by requiring written statements from both sides. The eight punishments administered by the Minister of Education to correct the myriad people were likewise detailed and comprehensive. Yet they still feared that ignorant people might fall into crime. Accordingly, they examined cases through the five modes of hearing, investigated them through the three consultations, and considered grounds for pardon through the three exemptions and three mitigations. Their instructions to exercise caution in adjudication and reverence in punishment richly embodied their house’s tradition of loyalty and generosity. Thereafter, the common people escaped punishment and execution, flourished in ritual propriety and righteousness, and left the prisons empty. What part of this was not nurtured by benevolent hearts and benevolent government? These four rulers’ virtue of cherishing life already prevailed before they put the laws in order, and their hearts, unable to bear others’ suffering, always extended their care even after the facts of a case had been established. When did they ever lightly contemplate a single punishment and thereby impair their compassionate benevolence? That this primal vitality of supreme harmony pervaded the world in the ages of Yu, Xia, and the flourishing Zhou is surely no false claim.
Once Zhou’s beneficent influence declined, laws and ordinances multiplied. Shen Buhai and Han Fei held sway in the Warring States period; Li Si and Zhao Gao pursued petty grievances under the Qin house of Ying. Those who voiced criticism were executed together with their clans; those who conversed in pairs were executed in the marketplace. The terror of punishment blazed while loyalty and consideration for others waned: these men merit no further discussion. Coming next to the Han, Emperor Gao reduced the laws to three articles, and Emperor Wen decreed the abolition of mutilating punishments. These measures were certainly sufficient to bind the people’s hearts to them and earn them recognition as worthy rulers of the Han…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
也然韓彭葅醢不免於寡恩薄昭伏誅則
失於慎始其後再傳而至武宣張湯趙禹
之徒進故縱連坐之法行一則繁刑多殺
一則啓釁基禍而漢家元氣剷削無餘可
勝嘆哉唐太宗奏必五覆幾致刑措矣然
君羨以圖讖含冤蘊古以直言被戮揆法
得無濫乎未幾而孽后司晨周興等盛開
告密致宗室大臣咸肝腦於酷吏之手夫
豈明刑之中也哉宋太宗親錄繫囚用法
===
平恕矣然武功以危疑自盡涪陵以私憾
貶死反巳寧無慚乎數傳而熙豐變法章
惇等恣為巧詆俾正人君子咸羅織於奸
黨之門夫豈貽謀之善也哉斯四君者或
狃於秦漢之習或溺於好惡之偏又安望
其恤民命致天和與前聖相脗合耶洪惟
我
太祖高皇帝以萬世綱常之主拯胡元憔悴之
民首命刑部尚書劉惟謙等重定諸律而
punctuated:
也。然韓彭葅醢，不免於寡恩；薄昭伏誅，則失於慎始。其後再傳而至武宣，張湯趙禹之徒進，故縱連坐之法行，一則繁刑多殺，一則啓釁基禍，而漢家元氣剷削無餘，可勝嘆哉！唐太宗奏必五覆，幾致刑措矣。然君羨以圖讖含冤，蘊古以直言被戮，揆法得無濫乎？未幾而孽后司晨，周興等盛開告密，致宗室大臣咸肝腦於酷吏之手，夫豈明刑之中也哉？宋太宗親錄繫囚，用法平恕矣。然武功以危疑自盡，涪陵以私憾貶死，反巳寧無慚乎？數傳而熙豐變法，章惇等恣為巧詆，俾正人君子咸羅織於奸黨之門，夫豈貽謀之善也哉？斯四君者，或狃於秦漢之習，或溺於好惡之偏，又安望其恤民命、致天和，與前聖相脗合耶？

洪惟我太祖高皇帝，以萬世綱常之主，拯胡元憔悴之民，首命刑部尚書劉惟謙等重定諸律，而
translation_en:
…indeed. Yet the pickling of Han Xin and Peng Yue as meat showed a lack of benevolence, while the execution of Bo Zhao revealed a failure to exercise caution at the outset. Two further successions brought the reigns of Emperors Wu and Xuan. Men such as Zhang Tang and Zhao Yu rose to prominence, and laws punishing the deliberate release of offenders and imposing collective liability came into force. On the one hand, punishments multiplied and executions abounded; on the other, these measures provoked strife and laid the foundations of disaster. The vital energies of the Han ruling house were utterly depleted. How could one lament this enough!

Emperor Taizong of Tang required five reviews of capital sentences submitted to him, almost bringing about a state in which punishments could be laid aside. Yet Junxian suffered injustice because of prophetic writings, and Yungu was executed for speaking frankly. Judged against the law, were these not abuses? Before long, a baleful empress assumed power, like a hen announcing the dawn. Zhou Xing and others opened wide the channels for secret denunciations, causing members of the imperial clan and high ministers alike to perish brutally at the hands of cruel officials. How could this represent the proper balance in making punishments clear?

Emperor Taizong of Song personally reviewed the cases of imprisoned suspects and applied the law impartially and leniently. Yet the Prince of Wugong took his own life amid peril and suspicion, while the Prince of Fuling was demoted out of personal resentment and died in exile. Could the emperor reflect upon himself without shame? Several reigns later came the reforms of the Xining and Yuanfeng eras. Zhang Dun and others freely devised cunning accusations, ensnaring upright men and gentlemen in charges of belonging to a treacherous faction. How could this be called sound planning for posterity?

These four rulers were either habituated to the practices of Qin and Han or submerged in the partiality of their likes and dislikes. How could one expect them to cherish the lives of the people, bring about Heaven’s harmony, and accord with the sages of old?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, sovereign guardian of the cardinal bonds and constant virtues for all ages, rescued the people left worn and wretched under the non-Chinese Yuan. He first ordered Liu Weiqian, Minister of Justice, and others to revise all the statutes, and…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
近代比例可資奸吏出入者咸痛革之緣
情定制務協厥中蓋唐宋以來所未有者
也及伏讀
祖訓一書申嚴大明律誥之守禁用黥刺剕劓
之刑至於
戒諭憲臣又有論法不當必傷善類之詞有
用藥或誤必致戕生之喻又曰鞫獄當平
恕自今民犯者毋連坐又曰善為國者惟
以好生樹德不以刑殺立威大哉
===
聖謨所以欽恤羣黎貽謀
億代者一何至也故仁心仁政浹洽於海宇
二百年來刑當其罪民安其生有由然矣
迨我
皇上以聰明仁聖之資撫
重熙累洽之運赦宥之條旣頒於
登極明詔矣茲當天下審決之期復
俞言官停免之請是心也卽天地好生之心也
舜禹成康欽恤之心也其與
punctuated:
近代比例可資奸吏出入者，咸痛革之。緣情定制，務協厥中，蓋唐宋以來所未有者也。及伏讀《祖訓》一書，申嚴《大明律》《誥》之守，禁用黥刺剕劓之刑。至於戒諭憲臣，又有「論法不當，必傷善類」之詞，有「用藥或誤，必致戕生」之喻。又曰：「鞫獄當平恕，自今民犯者毋連坐。」又曰：「善為國者，惟以好生樹德，不以刑殺立威。」大哉，聖謨！所以欽恤羣黎、貽謀億代者，一何至也！故仁心仁政浹洽於海宇，二百年來，刑當其罪，民安其生，有由然矣。
迨我皇上以聰明仁聖之資，撫重熙累洽之運，赦宥之條旣頒於登極明詔矣。茲當天下審決之期，復俞言官停免之請。是心也，卽天地好生之心也，舜禹成康欽恤之心也，其與
translation_en:
…he resolutely abolished all recent precedents and analogical rulings that could enable corrupt officials to manipulate liability for crimes. He established regulations in accordance with the circumstances of each offense, striving to attain the proper mean—something not seen since the Tang and Song dynasties. Moreover, on reverently reading the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun), I find that it insists upon strict observance of the Great Ming Code and the Pronouncements, and forbids the punishments of tattooing, amputation of the feet, and cutting off the nose. In admonishing censorial officials, he also declared, “Improper application of the law will inevitably harm good people,” and offered the analogy, “An error in administering medicine will inevitably destroy life.” He further said, “In investigating cases, be impartial and lenient. Henceforth, when commoners commit offenses, do not implicate others through collective liability.” Again he said, “Those who govern well establish virtue solely by cherishing life; they do not establish authority through punishment and execution.” How great these sagely counsels are! How consummate their provision for reverent care for the common people and guidance for countless generations! Thus his benevolent heart and benevolent government have permeated the realm. There is good reason why, for two hundred years, punishments have fitted crimes and the people have lived in security.
Now our Emperor, endowed with intelligence, benevolence, and sagely wisdom, presides over an age of continuing splendor and enduring harmony. Provisions for pardon and clemency have already been promulgated in the illustrious edict marking his accession. Now, at the time for reviewing cases and deciding executions throughout the realm, he has again approved the remonstrance officials’ request to suspend executions and grant exemptions. This heart is precisely the life-cherishing heart of Heaven and Earth, the heart of reverent compassion possessed by Shun, Yu, and Kings Cheng and Kang. In its relation to …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
皇祖慈祥之訓先後一揆故中外臣民躬逢
聖澤喜獲甦生莫不欣欣然歌詠太平矣有
君如此奚忍負之夫
恩詔渙頒其所以奉行者罔敢豫怠矣但
德意隆盛而推廣者庸有未周是故由憲臣以
及有司教以禮讓斷獄大減如韓延壽者
固不無其人矣然畫地不入刻木不對得
無如路溫舒之論於漢者乎獨存平恕不
施鞭扑如徐有功者固不無其人矣然失
===
入無辜失出為大罪得無如劉德威之論
於唐者乎至如緝捕以懲奸慝也乃今平
民瘐於鍛鍊一眚窮於文致卽
輦轂之下猶或有寃者況閭閻之遠者乎笞
杖本屬輕刑也乃今榜笞烈於炮烙性命
殞於箠楚卽內郡之臣猶或不免焉況荒
僻之陬乎夫匹夫結憤六月飛霜一婦含
寃三年不雨刑罰僭忒關係匪輕而苛吏
虐民者奚容於
punctuated: 皇祖慈祥之訓先後一揆，故中外臣民躬逢聖澤，喜獲甦生，莫不欣欣然歌詠太平矣。有君如此，奚忍負之？夫恩詔渙頒，其所以奉行者罔敢豫怠矣。但德意隆盛，而推廣者庸有未周。是故由憲臣以及有司，教以禮讓，斷獄大減，如韓延壽者，固不無其人矣。然畫地不入，刻木不對，得無如路溫舒之論於漢者乎？獨存平恕，不施鞭扑，如徐有功者，固不無其人矣。然失入無辜，失出為大罪，得無如劉德威之論於唐者乎？至如緝捕以懲奸慝也，乃今平民瘐於鍛鍊，一眚窮於文致，卽輦轂之下猶或有寃者，況閭閻之遠者乎？笞杖本屬輕刑也，乃今榜笞烈於炮烙，性命殞於箠楚，卽內郡之臣猶或不免焉，況荒僻之陬乎？夫匹夫結憤，六月飛霜；一婦含寃，三年不雨。刑罰僭忒，關係匪輕，而苛吏虐民者奚容於
translation_en: …accords throughout with the Imperial Ancestor’s teachings of kindness and compassion. Thus officials and common people, within the capital and beyond, personally receiving the sage sovereign’s favor and rejoicing in their deliverance, all gladly sing the praises of peaceful rule. With such a ruler, how could anyone bear to fail him? Now that the gracious edict has been widely promulgated, those charged with carrying it out dare not be idle or negligent. Yet, abundant though his virtuous intentions are, their extension may still be incomplete. Thus, among censorial officials and the responsible authorities, there are certainly men like Han Yanshou, who taught ritual propriety and deference and greatly reduced the number of cases requiring judgment. Yet people would not enter even a prison merely traced on the ground, nor answer even a jailer merely carved from wood: might conditions not resemble those discussed by Lu Wenshu under the Han? There are certainly also men like Xu Yougong, who upheld fairness and forbearance alone and did not employ whips or rods. Yet innocent people are wrongfully convicted, while wrongful acquittal is treated as a grave crime: might conditions not resemble those discussed by Liu Dewei under the Tang? As for pursuit and arrest, their purpose is to punish evildoers. Yet today ordinary people waste away in prison under the fabrication of charges, and a single fault brings utter ruin through strained constructions of the law. If some still suffer injustice even at the foot of the imperial carriage—in the capital itself—how much more must this be so in distant villages? Beating with the light bamboo and the heavy bamboo originally belonged to the lighter punishments. Yet today beatings are more ferocious than torture by burning, and lives are lost beneath the rods. If even officials in the interior commanderies sometimes cannot escape this, how much more must it occur in remote and desolate corners? When one common man harbored indignation, frost fell in the sixth month; when one woman suffered injustice, no rain fell for three years. Excesses and errors in punishment have consequences of no small moment. How, then, can harsh officials who torment the people be tolerated in…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
堯舜之世哉茲欲刑期無刑辟以止辟廣
皇仁以凝
天命宣惠政以恢
帝業當如何而後可亦曰重敎化清淹獄明律
例愼簡任而已夫帝舜之命契曰敬敷五
敎在寬其命臯陶曰明于五刑以弼五敎
則敎固刑之本也故必樹之軌則導之典
禮以啓其忠信之心以防其邪僻之念其
有不率敎者然後齊之以刑焉則民安於
===
爲善恥於犯法而比閭鮮爭鬪之獄矣崇
敎非所先乎夫夏月錄囚輕罪隨卽决遣
未能决者出獄聽候此
祖宗之恤典恩至厚也今各省有會審之例三
年有恤刑之官法亦備矣但郡縣獄犴每
遇天氣炎蒸之日類多病疫待斃之囚是
宜著爲令甲通行監司郡縣每年依期清
審輕罪如律决遣毋致久淹則囹圄無坐
斃之民矣清獄非所急乎夫罪有輕重吏
punctuated:
堯舜之世哉？茲欲刑期無刑，辟以止辟，廣皇仁以凝天命，宣惠政以恢帝業，當如何而後可？亦曰重敎化，清淹獄，明律例，愼簡任而已。夫帝舜之命契曰：「敬敷五敎，在寬。」其命臯陶曰：「明于五刑，以弼五敎。」則敎固刑之本也。故必樹之軌則，導之典禮，以啓其忠信之心，以防其邪僻之念。其有不率敎者，然後齊之以刑焉，則民安於爲善，恥於犯法，而比閭鮮爭鬪之獄矣。崇敎非所先乎？

夫夏月錄囚，輕罪隨卽决遣，未能决者出獄聽候，此祖宗之恤典，恩至厚也。今各省有會審之例，三年有恤刑之官，法亦備矣。但郡縣獄犴，每遇天氣炎蒸之日，類多病疫待斃之囚。是宜著爲令甲，通行監司郡縣，每年依期清審，輕罪如律决遣，毋致久淹，則囹圄無坐斃之民矣。清獄非所急乎？夫罪有輕重，吏
translation_en:
…in an age of Yao and Shun? Now, if we wish to employ punishment with the aim of eliminating punishment, and penalties to put an end to penalties, to extend imperial benevolence so as to secure Heaven’s Mandate, and to promulgate beneficent policies so as to expand the imperial enterprise, how can this be accomplished? Simply by giving weight to moral instruction, clearing long-pending prison cases, clarifying the statutes and substatutes, and exercising care in selecting and appointing officials. Emperor Shun commanded Xie: “Reverently spread the five teachings, doing so with leniency.” He commanded Gao Yao: “Apply the five punishments discerningly, to support the five teachings.” Instruction is thus indeed the foundation of punishment. We must therefore establish standards for the people and guide them through prescribed rites, awakening their loyalty and trustworthiness and guarding against wayward thoughts. Only those who fail to follow this instruction should then be brought into line through punishment. The people will thus be at ease in doing good and ashamed to violate the law, and cases arising from quarrels and fights will be rare in their neighborhoods. Is promoting instruction not the first priority?

In the summer months, prisoners’ cases are reviewed: those involving minor offenses are promptly decided and the prisoners discharged; those whose cases cannot yet be decided are released from prison to await a hearing. This compassionate provision of our imperial ancestors embodies the most generous benevolence. Today each province has provisions for joint judicial review, and every three years officials are dispatched to review criminal cases with a view to leniency. The arrangements are indeed comprehensive. Yet whenever the weather becomes oppressively hot, prefectural and county prisons commonly hold many prisoners who suffer from disease and epidemics and await death. A formal ordinance should therefore be issued to the regional supervisory authorities, prefectures, and counties, requiring them each year, at the prescribed time, to review and clear pending cases, promptly deciding minor offenses and discharging the prisoners according to law, without allowing prolonged detention. Then no one will die merely from languishing in prison. Is clearing prison cases not an urgent task? Offenses vary in gravity, and officials…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
有愛憎所欲活者傅生議所欲陷者比死
刑是受賕者得枉法以惠奸非辜者以深
文而抵罪即能控訴以自明然摩頂放踵
已不勝其荼毒矣謂宜申明律例如科條
未備者則爲之詳定其倫要如文義未明
者則爲之考訂其亂辭以頒布中外咸使
欽遵仍
勅諭問刑衙門凡有律例重而情狀輕者不得
妄行比附則法律畫一輕重有程而深刻
===
之吏又安得舞文操切耶夫張釋之爲廷
尉天下無冤民于定國爲廷尉民自以不
冤言在得人也今之獄吏擇之不可不精
任之不可不久察之不可不嚴是在撫按
督監司監司察守令其折獄明允蔚有仁
聲者則增秩賜金以責其成效然後破格
超遷以風勵乎庶職而乳虎蒼鷹羅鉗吉
網者即貶黜而重治之勿俾寅緣倖免則
守令皆循良而慘酷之吏又安得殘民以
punctuated:
有愛憎，所欲活者傅生議，所欲陷者比死刑，是受賕者得枉法以惠奸，非辜者以深文而抵罪。即能控訴以自明，然摩頂放踵，已不勝其荼毒矣。謂宜申明律例，如科條未備者，則爲之詳定其倫要；如文義未明者，則爲之考訂其亂辭，以頒布中外，咸使欽遵。仍勅諭問刑衙門，凡有律例重而情狀輕者，不得妄行比附，則法律畫一，輕重有程，而深刻之吏又安得舞文操切耶？
夫張釋之爲廷尉，天下無冤民；于定國爲廷尉，民自以不冤，言在得人也。今之獄吏，擇之不可不精，任之不可不久，察之不可不嚴。是在撫按督監司，監司察守令。其折獄明允、蔚有仁聲者，則增秩賜金，以責其成效，然後破格超遷，以風勵乎庶職。而乳虎蒼鷹、羅鉗吉網者，即貶黜而重治之，勿俾寅緣倖免，則守令皆循良，而慘酷之吏又安得殘民以
translation_en:
…have their likes and dislikes: for those they wish to keep alive, they contrive arguments for sparing their lives; for those they wish to bring down, they apply capital penalties by analogy. Thus those who accept bribes can pervert the law to favor evildoers, while the innocent are convicted through strained interpretations of the statutes. Even if they can appeal and clear themselves, they have already suffered unbearable torment from head to foot. I submit that the statutes and precedents should be clarified and reaffirmed. Where provisions are incomplete, their essential principles should be established in detail; where their wording is unclear, their confused language should be examined and corrected. They should then be promulgated throughout the capital and the provinces, so that all may reverently obey them. An imperial command should also instruct judicial offices that whenever the statutes and precedents prescribe severe penalties but the circumstances of the case are relatively minor, they must not recklessly apply provisions by analogy. The law would then be uniform, with established standards for the severity of punishments. How could harsh officials still manipulate its wording and oppress people?
When Zhang Shizhi served as Chamberlain for Law Enforcement, no one under Heaven suffered injustice; when Yu Dingguo held that office, the people themselves felt that they suffered no injustice. This shows that the essential thing is to find the right men. Judicial officials today must be selected with care, retained in office for a substantial time, and scrutinized rigorously. It falls to the grand coordinators and regional inspectors to oversee the surveillance commissioners, and to the surveillance commissioners to scrutinize the prefects and magistrates. Those whose judgments are discerning and fair, and who enjoy a flourishing reputation for benevolence, should receive increases in rank and gifts of money, while being held accountable for results. They should subsequently receive exceptional promotions beyond the normal rules, to encourage officials generally. But those who act like tigresses nursing their cubs or fierce hawks, employing ‘Luo’s pincers’ and ‘Ji’s net’ to entrap people, should immediately be demoted or dismissed and severely punished. They must not be allowed to escape through influence and connections [?]. Then prefects and magistrates would all govern conscientiously and benevolently; how could cruel officials still brutalize the people in order to…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
逞哉脩此四者則刑罰中而民心不惑聽
讞審而訟獄稱平肺石無晝籲之冤乾膚
得金矢之宜其所以擴
皇上好生之德而漸致刑措之治者豈淺淺哉
雖然猶有本焉書曰民心罔中惟爾之中
爾身克正罔敢不正孔子曰道之以德齊
之以禮有耻且格惟願我
皇上於端拱清穆之際切望道未見之誠主敬
以存此心務學以明此心親近君子以維
===
持此心則心正而身克脩矣由是正身以
正
朝廷以正百官以正萬民將見在朝成師讓
之風在野恊雍睦之化德教行而獄訟銷
自可措刑於不用矣此固端本澄源之道
竊有望於
今日者也惟執事采而行之幸甚
第三問
魏良臣
punctuated:
逞哉？脩此四者，則刑罰中而民心不惑，聽讞審而訟獄稱平，肺石無晝籲之冤，乾膚得金矢之宜。其所以擴皇上好生之德，而漸致刑措之治者，豈淺淺哉！雖然，猶有本焉。《書》曰：「民心罔中，惟爾之中。爾身克正，罔敢不正。」孔子曰：「道之以德，齊之以禮，有耻且格。」惟願我皇上於端拱清穆之際，切望道未見之誠，主敬以存此心，務學以明此心，親近君子以維持此心，則心正而身克脩矣。由是正身以正朝廷，以正百官，以正萬民，將見在朝成師讓之風，在野恊雍睦之化。德教行而獄訟銷，自可措刑於不用矣。此固端本澄源之道，竊有望於今日者也。惟執事采而行之，幸甚！

第三問
魏良臣
translation_en:
…vent their cruelty? If these four measures are carried out, punishments will be appropriate and the people’s hearts free from bewilderment; hearings and adjudications will be thorough, and litigation and criminal cases will be judged fairly. No one will cry out by day at the lung-stone with an unredressed grievance, and the handling of cases will attain the propriety signified by the dried flesh and the metal arrow. How could their contribution to extending His Majesty’s life-preserving virtue and gradually achieving a government in which punishments are laid aside be slight indeed? [The lung-stone was a place for petitioning against injustice; dried flesh and a metal arrow evoke the Book of Changes’ imagery of adjudication.]

Nevertheless, there is still a fundamental principle. The Book of Documents says: “The people’s hearts have no constant mean; they take your mean as their own. If you can make your own person upright, none will dare to be otherwise.” Confucius said: “Guide them through virtue and bring them into order through ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and rectify themselves.” I wish only that, amid the serene dignity of ruling with folded hands, His Majesty will earnestly seek the Way with the sincerity of one who has yet to behold it: maintaining reverence to preserve this mind, diligently pursuing learning to enlighten it, and drawing close to exemplary men to sustain it. Then his mind will be upright and his person can be cultivated. From this, by rectifying himself he will rectify the court, then all officials, and then all the people. We shall see a spirit of mutual deference [?] established at court and the transforming influence of concord and harmony spread among the people. As moral instruction takes effect and litigation disappears, punishments can naturally be laid aside unused. This is indeed the way to set the root right and clear the source; it is what I humbly hope for today. If you, honorable examiners, would adopt and implement these proposals, I should count it a great blessing.

Third Policy Question
Wei Liangchen

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
同考試官敎諭鄭批古今無不弊之法是在人
究極弊源變而通之耳經生遂能及此有用之學也錄之
同考試官敎授何批愼選擧公考課治天下之大端
也子能鑒古籌今卓有定見殆賈大夫而懷當世之慮者耶
考試官敎授吳批通達治體宜錄以式
考試官敎授李批博洽之學練達之才
賢才國家之利器也雖有良工器弗利則
無以善其事雖有明主賢弗用則罔與成
厥功甚哉賢才之有關於人國也用賢之
===
道其始也不有以招徠之何以盡天下之
才其旣也不有以甄別之何以成天下之
理是故養之欲豫擇之欲精則招徠之道
也辨之欲嚴核之欲實則甄別之術也擇
之精不才者不得以倖進核之實不肖者
不得以苟容持此以往而選擧考課之法
庶可以得眞才圖實効而國家尚亦有利
矣執事發策而擧二法以為問愚也方挾
策以就繩約何敢窺而議之雖然請誦所
punctuated:
同考試官敎諭鄭批：「古今無不弊之法，是在人究極弊源，變而通之耳。經生遂能及此，有用之學也，錄之。」

同考試官敎授何批：「愼選擧，公考課，治天下之大端也。子能鑒古籌今，卓有定見，殆賈大夫而懷當世之慮者耶？」

考試官敎授吳批：「通達治體，宜錄以式。」

考試官敎授李批：「博洽之學，練達之才。」

賢才，國家之利器也。雖有良工，器弗利則無以善其事；雖有明主，賢弗用則罔與成厥功。甚哉，賢才之有關於人國也！用賢之道，其始也，不有以招徠之，何以盡天下之才？其旣也，不有以甄別之，何以成天下之理？是故養之欲豫，擇之欲精，則招徠之道也；辨之欲嚴，核之欲實，則甄別之術也。擇之精，不才者不得以倖進；核之實，不肖者不得以苟容。持此以往，而選擧考課之法，庶可以得眞才，圖實効，而國家尚亦有利矣。執事發策而擧二法以為問，愚也方挾策以就繩約，何敢窺而議之？雖然，請誦所
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zheng, an Instructor, comments: “From antiquity to the present, no method has been free from defects. It rests with people to investigate the sources of those defects thoroughly and make changes so that the method works. That a student of the Classics should attain such understanding shows learning of practical use. Accept this essay.”

Associate Examiner He, a Professor, comments: “Careful selection and impartial performance evaluations are fundamental to governing the realm. You draw lessons from antiquity and deliberate on the present with remarkably firm judgment. Might you be another Grand Master Jia, concerned with the troubles of his age?”

Examiner Wu, a Professor, comments: “A thorough understanding of the principles of government. This should be included as a model.”

Examiner Li, a Professor, comments: “Broad and comprehensive learning; seasoned and capable talent.”

Worthy and talented men are the sharp instruments of the state. Even with a skilled craftsman, if his instruments are not sharp, he cannot do his work well; even with an enlightened ruler, if worthy men are not employed, he has no one with whom to accomplish his purposes. How profoundly worthy and talented men affect a state! In employing the worthy, if there is no means of attracting them at the outset, how can all the talent under Heaven be enlisted? If there is subsequently no means of distinguishing among them, how can orderly government be achieved throughout the realm? Thus, nurturing them in advance and selecting them with care are the means of attracting them; discriminating rigorously among them and assessing them on the basis of actual performance are the techniques of distinguishing among them. With careful selection, the untalented cannot advance through mere good fortune; with assessment based on actual performance, the unworthy cannot simply retain their positions. Proceeding on these principles, the methods of selection and performance evaluation may secure true talent and achieve practical results, bringing benefit to the state.

You, honored examiners, have issued a policy question concerning these two methods. I, in my ignorance, have only just come with my writings to submit to the prescribed standards; how dare I examine and discuss these matters? Nevertheless, permit me to recount what …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
聞以對夫天下可以一人有不可以一人
理書曰惟后非賢不乂言賢才之當用也
又曰知人則哲能官人言用人之當審也
惟用賢之爲急是故有選舉之法惟審用
之爲要是故有考課之法玆二法者其機
常相須而効實相因也無曠庶官天工人
其代之有功不賞有罪不罰雖堯舜不能
以爲理知乎此可以論治而語法矣選舉
之法何始乎自明揚師錫見於虞廷而求
===
賢之制其來遠矣然而莫備於周也周禮
大司徒以鄕三物敎萬民而賓興之三年
大比則合六鄕之民而考其德行道藝黨
正書之州長考之鄕大夫則以鄕飲酒禮
禮而賓之升之司徒升之司馬然後論定
而官焉其制詳且盡矣故一時得人稱爲
極盛而兔罝羔羊之咏非偶然也自是以
還漢詔郡國舉士之制不一而大槩有三
曰賢良方正也孝廉也博士弟子也賢良
punctuated:
聞以對。夫天下可以一人有，不可以一人理。《書》曰：「惟后非賢不乂。」言賢才之當用也。又曰：「知人則哲，能官人。」言用人之當審也。惟用賢之爲急，是故有選舉之法；惟審用之爲要，是故有考課之法。玆二法者，其機常相須，而効實相因也。「無曠庶官，天工人其代之。」有功不賞，有罪不罰，雖堯舜不能以爲理。知乎此，可以論治而語法矣。

選舉之法何始乎？自明揚師錫見於虞廷，而求賢之制其來遠矣。然而莫備於周也。《周禮》，大司徒以鄕三物敎萬民而賓興之。三年大比，則合六鄕之民而考其德行道藝。黨正書之，州長考之，鄕大夫則以鄕飲酒禮禮而賓之，升之司徒，升之司馬，然後論定而官焉。其制詳且盡矣。故一時得人，稱爲極盛，而《兔罝》《羔羊》之咏非偶然也。自是以還，漢詔郡國舉士之制不一，而大槩有三：曰賢良方正也，孝廉也，博士弟子也。賢良
translation_en:
…what I have heard, by way of reply. All under Heaven may be possessed by one person, but it cannot be governed by one person. The Book of Documents says: “The sovereign cannot bring order without worthy men.” This means that worthy and talented men must be employed. It also says: “To know men is wisdom; thus one can appoint men to office.” This means that one must exercise discernment in employing men. Because employing the worthy is urgent, there are methods of selection and recommendation; because careful discernment in their employment is essential, there are methods of evaluating officials’ performance. These two methods always depend upon one another in their operation, and their results are likewise interconnected. “Let none of the many offices remain unfilled: men are to perform Heaven’s work in its stead.” If merit is not rewarded and wrongdoing is not punished, even Yao and Shun could not bring about order. Understanding this, one may discuss government and its methods.

Where did the methods of selection and recommendation originate? Ever since the open promotion of men recommended by the assembled officials appeared at the court of Shun, institutions for seeking the worthy have had a long history. Yet nowhere were they more complete than under the Zhou. According to the Rites of Zhou, the Minister of Education taught the people through the three subjects of district instruction and advanced worthy men, honoring them as guests. At the great triennial assessment, the people of the six districts were assembled and examined for their virtue, conduct, knowledge of the Way, and arts. The Neighborhood Head recorded these qualities, and the Township Head assessed them. The District Grand Master then honored the candidates as guests through the district drinking ceremony and advanced them to the Minister of Education, who advanced them to the Minister of War. Only after deliberation and a final determination were they appointed to office. This system was detailed and comprehensive. Thus that age was acclaimed as the height of success in obtaining worthy men, and the praises sung in “The Rabbit Net” and “The Lamb’s Fur” were no accident. Thereafter, under the Han, imperial edicts established various procedures by which commanderies and kingdoms recommended men. Broadly speaking, there were three categories: the Worthy and Good, Upright and Correct; the Filial and Incorrupt; and Disciples of the Erudites. The Worthy and Good…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
孝廉舉以任用若周官之進士博土弟子
入補國學若周官之俊士猶有德行之遺
意焉唐之科目雖多而行之最久者有二
曰明經也進士也進士以聲韻爲學不本
經術明經以帖誦爲能不窮義理所謂德
行者不復問矣宋初猶並用二科至王安
石乃盡廢諸科令士各占治易詩書周禮
禮記一經兼以論語孟子毎試四場經義
以探其學術論策以考其智慮且曰欲以
===
一道德而同風俗也漢唐宋之法皆能得
人要而求之則宋中更之制有不可廢者
蓋漢制近古而今則難行唐制尚文而實
則未競宋則變聲律爲議論變墨義爲大
義而發策决科之士庶幾有誦聖賢之遺
言而窺其用心者此其法之可取也雖未
可方成周三物之敎而後世之制則爲彼
善矣考課之法何始乎自敷奏明試之典
見於虞廷而課功之制其來遠矣然而莫
punctuated:
孝廉舉以任用，若周官之進士；博土弟子入補國學，若周官之俊士，猶有德行之遺意焉。唐之科目雖多，而行之最久者有二，曰明經也，進士也。進士以聲韻爲學，不本經術；明經以帖誦爲能，不窮義理。所謂德行者，不復問矣。宋初猶並用二科，至王安石，乃盡廢諸科，令士各占治《易》《詩》《書》《周禮》《禮記》一經，兼以《論語》《孟子》。毎試四場，經義以探其學術，論策以考其智慮，且曰：「欲以一道德而同風俗也。」漢唐宋之法皆能得人，要而求之，則宋中更之制有不可廢者。蓋漢制近古，而今則難行；唐制尚文，而實則未競；宋則變聲律爲議論，變墨義爲大義，而發策决科之士，庶幾有誦聖賢之遺言而窺其用心者。此其法之可取也。雖未可方成周三物之敎，而後世之制，則爲彼善矣。

考課之法何始乎？自敷奏明試之典見於虞廷，而課功之制，其來遠矣。然而莫
translation_en:
…and those recommended for filial piety and integrity were selected for appointment, like the “advanced scholars” in the Offices of Zhou. Students of the Erudites [博土, apparently 博士] entered the state school to fill vacancies, like the “outstanding scholars” in the Offices of Zhou. These arrangements still retained something of the ancient emphasis on virtuous conduct. Although the Tang had many examination categories, the two maintained longest were “Illuminating the Classics” (mingjing) and “Presented Scholar” (jinshi). Candidates in the latter made sounds and rhymes their study, without grounding themselves in classical learning; candidates in the former made proficiency in filling blanks in classical passages and recitation their accomplishment, without thoroughly investigating meaning and principle. Virtuous conduct, as it was called, was no longer inquired into.

At the beginning of the Song, both categories continued to be used. With Wang Anshi, however, all the various categories were abolished, and scholars were required each to declare one classic as their specialization—the Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites of Zhou, or Record of Rites—together with the Analects and Mencius. Each examination comprised four sessions: essays on the meaning of the classics investigated their learning, while discourses and policy essays tested their judgment and deliberation. He further declared: “The intention is thereby to unify moral understanding and make customs uniform.”

The methods of the Han, Tang, and Song all succeeded in obtaining capable men. On examining their essentials, however, certain features of the system revised during the Song cannot be dispensed with. The Han system approached antiquity, but would now be difficult to implement. The Tang system prized literary accomplishment, but its substance was not fully developed [?]. The Song replaced tonal and metrical composition with reasoned discussion, and written questions on textual details with essays on broader meaning. Among those who answered policy questions and thereby secured examination success, there might thus be some who recited the words bequeathed by the sages and worthies and discerned the intentions behind them. This is what merits adoption in that method. Although it cannot yet be compared with the mature Zhou’s teaching through the three categories, it is the better among the systems of later ages.

Where did the method of evaluating officials’ performance begin? Since the practice of having officials present their accounts and clearly testing them appears in the court of Shun, the system of assessing accomplishments has a long history. Yet none…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
備於周也周禮太宰掌計羣吏之治終嵗
之間旬有日成月有月要嵗有嵗會百官
各正其治受其會聽其致事而詔其廢置
三嵗則大計而誅賞之聽之以六計馭之
以八柄而淑慝于是乎分焉其法精且密
矣故當時在位罔非吉士而咸和永清之
化有由然也自是以降漢以六條按郡國
曰强豪踰制曰背公向私曰不卹疑獄曰
選署不平曰恃勢請託曰違公損下所謂
===
六條也唐以九等課百司敘之以四善曰
德義有聞曰清謹名著曰公平可稱曰恪
勤匪懈而緯之以二十七最自近侍至於
鎮防一最四善爲上上一最三善爲上中
一最二善爲上下無最而有二善爲中上
無最而有一善爲中中職事粗理善最不
聞爲中下愛憎任情處斷乖理爲下上背
公向私職務廢缺爲下中居官諂詐貪得
有狀爲下下所謂九等也宋以七事考轉
punctuated:
備於周也。《周禮》，太宰掌計羣吏之治。終嵗之間，旬有日成，月有月要，嵗有嵗會。百官各正其治，受其會，聽其致事，而詔其廢置。三嵗則大計而誅賞之，聽之以六計，馭之以八柄，而淑慝于是乎分焉。其法精且密矣，故當時在位罔非吉士，而咸和永清之化有由然也。

自是以降，漢以六條按郡國：曰强豪踰制，曰背公向私，曰不卹疑獄，曰選署不平，曰恃勢請託，曰違公損下，所謂六條也。

唐以九等課百司，敘之以四善：曰德義有聞，曰清謹名著，曰公平可稱，曰恪勤匪懈。而緯之以二十七最，自近侍至於鎮防。一最四善爲上上，一最三善爲上中，一最二善爲上下；無最而有二善爲中上，無最而有一善爲中中，職事粗理、善最不聞爲中下；愛憎任情、處斷乖理爲下上，背公向私、職務廢缺爲下中，居官諂詐、貪得有狀爲下下。所謂九等也。

宋以七事考轉
translation_en:
… as comprehensive as under the Zhou. According to the Rites of Zhou, the Grand Steward was responsible for assessing the administration of all officials. Throughout the year, each ten-day period had its daily tallies, each month its monthly summaries, and each year its annual accounts. The officials each put their administration in order; the Grand Steward received their accounts, heard their reports on completed business, and advised the ruler on their dismissal or retention. Every three years, he conducted a comprehensive assessment and imposed punishments or rewards. He judged them by six criteria and governed them through eight instruments of authority, thereby distinguishing the good from the wicked. These procedures were precise and thorough. Thus, those holding office at the time were all worthy men: this explains how the transforming influence of government brought universal harmony and enduring tranquillity.

Thereafter, the Han inspected the commanderies and kingdoms according to six articles: powerful local magnates exceeding prescribed limits; turning away from public duty toward private interests; failing to give due care to doubtful criminal cases; unfairness in selection and appointment; relying on influence to solicit favors; and violating the public interest and harming subordinates. These were the so-called six articles.

The Tang assessed the various offices using nine grades. Officials were ranked according to four virtues: a reputation for moral integrity and righteousness; recognized incorruptibility and circumspection; praiseworthy fairness and impartiality; and conscientious diligence without slackening. These were combined with twenty-seven categories of outstanding performance, covering offices from personal attendants to garrison defense. One distinction for outstanding performance and four virtues earned the highest grade in the upper class; one distinction and three virtues, the middle grade in the upper class; and one distinction and two virtues, the lowest grade in the upper class. No distinction but two virtues earned the highest grade in the middle class; no distinction but one virtue, the middle grade in the middle class; and merely adequate management of official duties, without any recognized virtue or distinction, the lowest grade in the middle class. Giving free rein to personal likes and dislikes and making unreasonable decisions earned the highest grade in the lower class; turning away from public duty toward private interests and neglecting official responsibilities, the middle grade in the lower class; and practicing flattery and deceit in office, with demonstrable instances of corrupt acquisition, the lowest grade in the lower class. These were the so-called nine grades.

The Song used seven criteria to assess transport …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
運提舉等官曰舉官曰勸農桑曰招流亡
曰興利除害曰案察部吏贓罪曰平反獄
訟曰覺察盜賊所謂七事也以九事考校
縣令曰斷獄平允曰賦稅不擾曰差徭均
曰盜賊屏曰勸農曰恤孤寡曰修水利曰
户口增衍曰整治簿書所謂九事也漢唐
宋之法皆能致治然漢制主於按劾近於
刻峭宋制詳於文法失之重複唐則善以
著其德行最以著其才術以善與最相爲
===
乘除分爲九等上者加階其次進祿其下
奪祿又其下解任詳於善而略於最此其
法之可取也雖非成周大計之治而後世
之制則爲彼善矣洪惟我
朝損益前代之制著立一定之法其取士也
旣羣之學校以養之矣乃董之以師儒督
之以憲臣而就試之制則倣宋儒所謂貢
舉私議者三年大比登俊於鄉卽鄉大夫
之興禮也上之禮闈以俟
punctuated:
運、提舉等官，曰舉官，曰勸農桑，曰招流亡，曰興利除害，曰案察部吏贓罪，曰平反獄訟，曰覺察盜賊，所謂七事也。以九事考校縣令，曰斷獄平允，曰賦稅不擾，曰差徭均，曰盜賊屏，曰勸農，曰恤孤寡，曰修水利，曰户口增衍，曰整治簿書，所謂九事也。漢、唐、宋之法皆能致治，然漢制主於按劾，近於刻峭；宋制詳於文法，失之重複；唐則善以著其德行，最以著其才術，以善與最相爲乘除，分爲九等。上者加階，其次進祿，其下奪祿，又其下解任。詳於善而略於最，此其法之可取也。雖非成周大計之治，而後世之制則爲彼善矣。
洪惟我朝損益前代之制，著立一定之法。其取士也，旣羣之學校以養之矣，乃董之以師儒，督之以憲臣；而就試之制，則倣宋儒所謂《貢舉私議》者。三年大比，登俊於鄉，卽鄉大夫之興禮也。上之禮闈，以俟
translation_en:
…Transport Commissioners, Superintendents, and other officials: recommending officials; encouraging agriculture and sericulture; bringing back displaced people; promoting benefits and eliminating harms; investigating corruption among subordinate officials; reviewing judicial cases and redressing wrongful judgments; and detecting bandits and thieves. These were the so-called seven duties. Magistrates were assessed on nine duties: deciding cases fairly; collecting taxes without harassing the people; distributing labor service equitably; suppressing bandits and thieves; encouraging agriculture; caring for orphans and widows; maintaining irrigation works; increasing the number of households and inhabitants; and putting registers and documents in order. These were the so-called nine duties.
The methods of the Han, Tang, and Song could all produce good government. Yet the Han system emphasized investigation and impeachment, tending toward excessive severity; the Song system elaborated documentary rules, erring through duplication. Under the Tang, ratings for goodness demonstrated an official’s moral conduct, while ratings for outstanding achievement demonstrated his ability and skill. These two kinds of ratings were weighed against one another to establish nine grades. Those in the highest grades received advancement in rank; those next below received increased stipends; those further below lost stipends; and those still lower were dismissed. Its detailed treatment of goodness and comparatively brief treatment of outstanding achievement were the commendable features of this method. Although it did not attain the governance achieved through the comprehensive assessments of the Zhou, it was the better of the systems of later ages.
We reverently reflect that our dynasty has modified the institutions of preceding ages and established a fixed body of regulations. In recruiting scholars, it first gathers them in schools to nurture them, then places them under the guidance of learned teachers and the supervision of censorial officials. Its examination system follows what a Song Confucian scholar called Personal Proposals on Recruitment by Recommendation and Examination (Gongju siyi). Every three years, a great assessment raises up outstanding men through the Provincial Examination: this corresponds to the ceremony by which the Zhou District Grand Masters promoted worthy men. They are then sent onward to the examination precincts of the Ministry of Rites, to await…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
廷對卽大司馬之進士也此蓋本虞周之意
而兼漢唐宋之美一代士類之進濟濟乎
明揚賓興之盛矣其課吏也旣分之職事
以責之矣乃糾之以監司統之以臺省而
考語所書則取唐人所爲等其善最者九
年通考第其升降卽虞廷之考績也三載
述事大明黜陟卽周官之大計也此蓋監
虞周之制而集漢唐宋之成一代吏治之
飭翼翼乎慶賞刑威之嚴矣二百年于茲
===
名卿碩輔于是乎出內輯外寧于是乎效
孰非選舉考課之美而得人維治之功哉
是宜萬世遵行永遠無弊固無以議爲者
然而論者猶以科舉之文不適實用考課
之法未免失眞愚則以爲非法之弊也有
治人無治法存乎其人焉耳夫所善於選
舉者爲其無失人也然用法之精在人而
不在法是非邪正吾懸鑑以照之則雖用
今之法而自可以得人不必其合於古否
punctuated:
廷對，卽大司馬之進士也。此蓋本虞周之意，而兼漢唐宋之美，一代士類之進，濟濟乎明揚賓興之盛矣。
其課吏也，旣分之職事以責之矣，乃糾之以監司，統之以臺省，而考語所書，則取唐人所爲等其善最者。九年通考，第其升降，卽虞廷之考績也；三載述事，大明黜陟，卽周官之大計也。此蓋監虞周之制，而集漢唐宋之成，一代吏治之飭，翼翼乎慶賞刑威之嚴矣。二百年于茲，名卿碩輔于是乎出，內輯外寧于是乎效，孰非選舉考課之美，而得人維治之功哉！是宜萬世遵行，永遠無弊，固無以議爲者。
然而論者猶以科舉之文不適實用，考課之法未免失眞。愚則以爲非法之弊也，有治人，無治法，存乎其人焉耳。夫所善於選舉者，爲其無失人也。然用法之精，在人而不在法。是非邪正，吾懸鑑以照之，則雖用今之法，而自可以得人，不必其合於古否
translation_en:
…to respond at court: this corresponds to the Grand Minister of War’s advancement of worthy men. This system takes its underlying purpose from the ages of Shun and Zhou while incorporating the strengths of Han, Tang, and Song. In advancing the scholars of our dynasty, how abundant is its flourishing array of worthies, publicly recognized and ceremonially received as guests!
As for evaluating officials, they are first assigned distinct duties and held accountable for them; they are then scrutinized by supervisory officials and placed under the oversight of the Censorate and central ministries. The written assessments adopt the Tang practice of grading officials by their virtues and outstanding achievements. Comprehensive evaluation after nine years, determining their promotion or demotion, corresponds to the performance evaluations at Shun’s court. Reporting accomplishments every three years and clearly determining dismissal or advancement corresponds to the great reckoning of the Offices of Zhou. This system takes the institutions of Shun and Zhou as its model and brings together the accomplishments of Han, Tang, and Song. In regulating official administration throughout our dynasty, how scrupulously it maintains the rigor of rewards and punishments! Over these two hundred years, eminent ministers and great counselors have emerged through it, and internal harmony and external peace have resulted from it. Which of these is not the fruit of excellent selection and evaluation, and of securing worthy men to sustain good government? Such institutions should indeed be followed for ten thousand generations, remaining forever free of defects; there would assuredly be no grounds for criticism.
Yet critics still maintain that examination compositions are unsuited to practical use and that the methods of evaluating officials do not altogether escape misrepresentation. In my humble view, these are not defects of the institutions. There are men who bring about good government, but no methods that do so of themselves: everything rests with the men concerned. What we value in selection is that it should overlook no worthy person. Yet precision in applying its methods rests with people, not with the methods themselves. If we hang up a mirror to illuminate right and wrong, the crooked and the upright, then even by using today’s methods we can naturally secure worthy men, without its being necessary to ask whether they accord with antiquity…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
也所善於考課者爲其無失事也然用法
之核在人而不在法進退黜陟吾持衡以
平之則雖用今之法而亦可以課吏不必
其合於古否也何也科目不足以得士則
將舍此而鄉舉里選乎風氣日流奸僞日
甚卽今試法之嚴猶恐僥濫厠迹爲清議
訾使壹用辟召是開弊竇而長倖梯也夫
科目之累人非科目之累也學術之不正
使之也今之應舉者有不誦法聖賢者乎
===
窮經而致用世未嘗乏人也然務勦說而
鮮自得軼師傳而詭時好者亦時有之宜
乎識者有虛名亡實之憂也雖然亦明以
辨之而已根理之學不飾而妍枝葉之辭
雖工亦厭詖淫邪遁者必斥勿長浮薄之
風典雅朴茂者必錄冀收沉實之用如是
其於人材真僞亦庶幾乎拔十得五矣有
不足爲世道之助乎考課慮其失真則將
如虞廷三考而後黜陟耶虐政害民朝弗
punctuated: 也。所善於考課者，爲其無失事也。然用法之核，在人而不在法。進退黜陟，吾持衡以平之，則雖用今之法，而亦可以課吏，不必其合於古否也。何也？科目不足以得士，則將舍此而鄉舉里選乎？風氣日流，奸僞日甚，卽今試法之嚴，猶恐僥濫厠迹，爲清議訾。使壹用辟召，是開弊竇而長倖梯也。夫科目之累人，非科目之累也，學術之不正使之也。今之應舉者，有不誦法聖賢者乎？窮經而致用，世未嘗乏人也。然務勦說而鮮自得，軼師傳而詭時好者，亦時有之。宜乎識者有虛名亡實之憂也。雖然，亦明以辨之而已。根理之學，不飾而妍；枝葉之辭，雖工亦厭。詖淫邪遁者必斥，勿長浮薄之風；典雅朴茂者必錄，冀收沉實之用。如是，其於人材真僞，亦庶幾乎拔十得五矣。有不足爲世道之助乎？考課慮其失真，則將如虞廷三考而後黜陟耶？虐政害民，朝弗
translation_en:
…What is commendable about performance evaluations is that they prevent official duties from being neglected. Yet rigorous application of the rules depends on the people administering them, not on the rules themselves. If we hold the balance even in advancing and retiring, dismissing and promoting officials, then even the present rules can serve to evaluate them; they need not conform to those of antiquity. Why is this? If the examination system cannot secure worthy scholars, are we to abandon it for nomination by districts and selection by villages? Customs deteriorate daily, and deceit grows ever worse. Even with the strict examination rules now in force, we still fear that undeserving men may slip into the ranks through luck or abuse, provoking the censure of informed public opinion. To rely exclusively on recruitment by invitation would open loopholes for malpractice and provide a ladder for advancement by luck.

When the examination system burdens men, the fault does not lie in the system itself: it results from unsound learning. Among those now taking the examinations, is there anyone who does not recite the teachings of the sages and worthies and take them as models? The world has never lacked men who thoroughly investigate the Classics and put their learning to practical use. Yet there are also, from time to time, those who devote themselves to plagiarizing explanations and gain little understanding of their own, departing from their teachers’ transmitted learning and catering deviously to current tastes [?]. No wonder discerning men worry about empty reputations devoid of substance. Nevertheless, all that is needed is clear discernment. Learning rooted in principle is beautiful without adornment; language consisting merely of branches and leaves is tiresome even when skillfully composed. Those whose words are biased, excessive, perverse, or evasive must be rejected, lest a shallow and frivolous style flourish. Those whose writing is refined, correct, plain, and substantial must be selected, in the hope of securing the service of steady and practical men. In this way, when distinguishing genuine talent from false, we might come close to finding five worthy men among every ten selected. Would this not help improve the condition of the world?

If we fear that performance evaluations fail to reflect the truth, are we then to follow the court of Shun and wait for three evaluations before dismissing or promoting officials? When oppressive government harms the people, from morning one cannot…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
及夕卽今法網之密猶恐竒袤逸罰爲治
體累使更用疏闊是滋官邪而重民患也
夫考課之病治非考課之病也稱量之弗
協使之也今之服官者有不顧畏名義者
乎爲善而務實世未嘗乏人也然背公義
而植私交飾僞價而徼市利者亦或有之
宜乎識者有任法失人之懼也雖然亦公
以持之而已賢者必進不以私抑不肖者
必退不以情免悃愊無華者毋以悶悶而
===
遺其賢奔競爲悅者毋以矯矯而没其不
肖如是其於人材之進退亦庶幾乎十不
失一矣有不足爲治典之光乎抑猶未也
今之選擧旣竭其明矣而執事猶遺賢是
懼惓惓之誠是也愚則以方今之士景附響
從視古之鄕擧里選不啻盛矣合網羅而
囊括之一藝一能無不自效而豈遺賢之
患雖然有一說焉取士以試應試以文而
賢能所儲初不在是也必也明敎化乎今
punctuated:
及夕。卽今法網之密，猶恐竒袤逸罰，爲治體累；使更用疏闊，是滋官邪而重民患也。夫考課之病治，非考課之病也，稱量之弗協使之也。今之服官者，有不顧畏名義者乎？爲善而務實，世未嘗乏人也。然背公義而植私交，飾僞價而徼市利者，亦或有之。宜乎識者有任法失人之懼也。雖然，亦公以持之而已。賢者必進，不以私抑；不肖者必退，不以情免。悃愊無華者，毋以悶悶而遺其賢；奔競爲悅者，毋以矯矯而没其不肖。如是，其於人材之進退，亦庶幾乎十不失一矣。有不足爲治典之光乎？
抑猶未也。今之選擧，旣竭其明矣，而執事猶遺賢是懼，惓惓之誠是也。愚則以方今之士景附響從，視古之鄕擧里選，不啻盛矣。合網羅而囊括之，一藝一能，無不自效，而豈遺賢之患？雖然，有一說焉：取士以試，應試以文，而賢能所儲，初不在是也。必也明敎化乎！今
translation_en:
…last until evening. Even with the close mesh of the law today, there is still fear that wrongdoers [?] will escape punishment and impair the system of government. To make it still looser would foster official misconduct and compound the people’s suffering. When performance evaluations harm government, the fault does not lie in evaluation itself; it arises from improper assessment. Among those now holding office, are there any who have no regard or fear for reputation and duty? The world has never lacked people who do good and devote themselves to substantive achievement. Yet there are also some who turn their backs on public duty to cultivate private connections, inflate their worth with false appearances, and seek gain as in a marketplace. It is understandable that discerning men fear that reliance on regulations may lead to mistaken judgments of people. Nevertheless, all that is needed is to administer them impartially. The worthy must be advanced, never held back for private reasons; the unworthy must be dismissed, never spared out of personal affection. Do not overlook the worth of sincere, unadorned men because they seem dull; do not let the conspicuous bearing of men who scramble for advancement and seek to please conceal their unworthiness. In this way, in advancing and dismissing men of talent, one might approach a record of not a single mistake in ten. Would this not lend distinction to the institutions of government?
Yet this is still not enough. In selecting men today, you have already exercised your discernment to the utmost, but you still fear overlooking worthy men: this shows your earnest sincerity. In my humble view, scholars today attach themselves like shadows and respond like echoes; their numbers are more than a match for those recommended by districts and selected by villages in antiquity. They should all be gathered in and embraced, so that anyone possessing even one skill or ability can offer his services. What fear would there then be of overlooking the worthy? Nevertheless, there is one further point: men are recruited through examinations, and they answer examinations with literary compositions, but these are not, in the first place, where worth and ability reside. Surely moral instruction must be made clear! Now …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
夫樹棘者得刺樹果者得實養之貴以豫
也周官選舉之法敎以德行使民興賢敎
以道藝使民興能興賢則出使長之興能
則入使治之是以民無弗服而事無弗理
眞才可得而用也今也師儒之所敎憲臣
之所督非不曰德行道藝也然誘之以利
祿之途敎之以文字之學所重固有在矣
誘之使來而復禁其趨敎之已成而顧違
其用是所望非所樹也必不然矣竊以為
===
養士者必重師儒之選而申本實之敎課
之以經義則校其躬行而不徒采其華課
之以世務必求其實用而不徒騰其說德
行道藝彬彬可睹如胡瑗所謂經義治事
者然後學官書其績憲臣攷其成雖科目
所舉專以其文而行藝之脩則旣備矣異
日之所使卽今日之所敎尚何人材之不
可用而遺賢是虞乎是故科舉莫先於明
敎化也今之考課旣極其公矣而執事猶
punctuated:
夫樹棘者得刺，樹果者得實，養之貴以豫也。《周官》選舉之法，敎以德行，使民興賢；敎以道藝，使民興能。興賢則出使長之，興能則入使治之。是以民無弗服，而事無弗理，眞才可得而用也。今也師儒之所敎、憲臣之所督，非不曰德行道藝也。然誘之以利祿之途，敎之以文字之學，所重固有在矣。誘之使來，而復禁其趨；敎之已成，而顧違其用，是所望非所樹也，必不然矣。竊以為，養士者必重師儒之選，而申本實之敎。課之以經義，則校其躬行，而不徒采其華；課之以世務，必求其實用，而不徒騰其說。德行道藝彬彬可睹，如胡瑗所謂經義治事者，然後學官書其績，憲臣攷其成。雖科目所舉專以其文，而行藝之脩則旣備矣。異日之所使，卽今日之所敎，尚何人材之不可用，而遺賢是虞乎？是故科舉莫先於明敎化也。

今之考課旣極其公矣，而執事猶
translation_en:
Those who plant brambles obtain thorns; those who plant fruit trees obtain fruit. In nurturing talent, preparation beforehand is essential. Under the selection system of the Offices of Zhou, people were taught virtue and conduct and encouraged to recommend the worthy; they were taught the Way and practical arts and encouraged to recommend the capable. Those recommended for worthiness were sent out to lead the people; those recommended for ability were brought in to administer affairs. Thus none among the people failed to submit, and no affairs went unmanaged: genuine talent could be found and employed. Today, what teachers teach and censorial officials supervise is indeed called virtue, conduct, the Way, and practical arts. Yet students are enticed with the prospect of profit and official emoluments and instructed in literary composition. What is actually valued is clear enough. To entice them to come, then forbid them to pursue that path; to complete their education, then employ them contrary to their training—this is to expect something other than what one has planted. It surely cannot work.

I humbly believe that those who nurture scholars must give weight to the selection of teachers and reinforce instruction in fundamentals and substance. When examining students on the meaning of the classics, they should assess how students put it into practice themselves, rather than merely prize literary ornament. When examining them on contemporary affairs, they must seek practical applicability, rather than merely encourage the airing of theories. Virtue, conduct, the Way, and practical arts should be manifest in balanced cultivation, as in what Hu Yuan called the study of classical meaning and the management of affairs. Then education officials should record their achievements, and censorial officials assess their accomplishments. Although selection through the examinations depends exclusively on their writing, their cultivation of conduct and skills will already be complete. What they are employed to do in the future will be precisely what they are taught today. Why then should there be any concern that talented men cannot be employed, or that worthy men have been overlooked? Thus, in the examination system, nothing takes precedence over making moral instruction clear.

The present assessment of officials has already attained the utmost impartiality, yet you gentlemen still…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
倖位是懼懼之誠是也愚則以方今之法
毫舉櫛剔視周官之日成月要不啻密矣
挽江河而洒滌之一垢一瘢無不立見而
何倖位之有雖然有一說焉立法貴嚴持
法貴公而賢否之辨則不係是也必也核
名實乎今夫稱農者視其穀稱牧者視其
畜察之各以業也周官考課之法有待其
治者以定其始有逆其治者以稽其終待
於先即以責驗其終逆於後即以鉤考其
===
始是以其實無所遯而其虚不可飾眞才
可得而見也今也進賢如恐弗勝退不肖
如恐弗及非不日較著章明也然因人言
以為進退采風聞以定是非勢亦有不免
矣人情有愛憎而言未必公風聞多影響
而事未必實此為所察非所業也必不得
矣竊以為課吏者必核其職業之守而擴
吾通闗之見其事治其民安非貪慢之吏
所能辦也毀之者勿聽其事不治其民不
punctuated:
倖位是懼。懼之誠是也。愚則以方今之法，毫舉櫛剔，視周官之日成月要，不啻密矣。挽江河而洒滌之，一垢一瘢，無不立見，而何倖位之有？雖然，有一說焉：立法貴嚴，持法貴公，而賢否之辨則不係是也。必也核名實乎！今夫稱農者視其穀，稱牧者視其畜，察之各以業也。周官考課之法，有待其治者以定其始，有逆其治者以稽其終。待於先，即以責驗其終；逆於後，即以鉤考其始。是以其實無所遯，而其虚不可飾，眞才可得而見也。

今也進賢如恐弗勝，退不肖如恐弗及，非不日較著章明也。然因人言以為進退，采風聞以定是非，勢亦有不免矣。人情有愛憎，而言未必公；風聞多影響，而事未必實。此為所察非所業也，必不得矣。竊以為課吏者，必核其職業之守，而擴吾通闗之見。其事治，其民安，非貪慢之吏所能辦也，毀之者勿聽；其事不治，其民不
translation_en:
…fear that men may occupy office through undeserved good fortune. Such fear is indeed justified. In my humble view, however, present regulations examine every hair’s breadth and sift matters as finely as a comb; compared with the daily accounts and monthly summaries prescribed in the Offices of Zhou, they are more than sufficiently exacting. It is as though the waters of great rivers were drawn upon to wash everything clean: every speck of dirt and every blemish immediately becomes visible. How, then, could anyone occupy office undeservedly? Nevertheless, there is something further to say. In establishing regulations, strictness is essential; in applying them, impartiality is essential. Yet distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy does not depend upon these alone. Surely one must examine whether reputation accords with actual performance! If someone is called a farmer, we inspect his grain; if someone is called a herdsman, we inspect his livestock. Each is examined according to his occupation. The methods of evaluating officials in the Offices of Zhou include anticipating their administration so as to establish its initial terms, and reviewing their administration so as to assess its conclusion. Expectations established beforehand provide the basis for demanding verification of the eventual results; retrospective review provides the means to investigate the original undertaking. Thus actual performance has nowhere to hide, empty pretensions cannot be embellished, and genuine ability can be discerned.

Today, worthy men are promoted as though one feared being unable to promote them all, and unworthy men are dismissed as though one feared acting too late. It is not that these distinctions are not made increasingly evident each day. Yet circumstances sometimes make it unavoidable that promotion and dismissal depend on what others say, and that judgments of right and wrong rest on hearsay. Human feelings involve affection and aversion, so statements are not necessarily impartial; hearsay often consists of shadows and echoes, so the reported facts are not necessarily true. This means that what is examined is not the person’s actual work; sound judgment therefore cannot be obtained [?]. I humbly believe that those who evaluate officials must examine how they discharge their official duties and broaden their own comprehensive understanding [?]. If an official’s affairs are well administered and his people are at peace, this is something a greedy or negligent official could not accomplish: do not listen to those who malign him. If his affairs are not well administered and his people are not…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
安非廉明之吏所宜有也譽之者亦勿聽
事蹟功罪斷斷不渝如齊威所爲烹阿封
卽墨者斯則名不以疏逖而不章實不以
彌縫而可匿雖課典之行裁之自我而情
狀在彼則旣悉矣飾名不得以求功巧文
不得以逃罪尚何吏治之不可飭而倖位
是憂乎是故考課莫貴乎核名實也噫敎
化行則舉不失人而吾之明益著名實核
則法無倖免而吾之公益彰明以擇之於
===
先不才者不得以倖進公以核之於後倖
進者不得以苟容賢者進則庶職脩矣不
肖者不容則治道粹矣明主恭己而無爲
大臣布公而弘化率是道也故夫師古之
意而不泥其法由今之法而獲古之治惟
公與明者得之若夫下之自處則如之何
學患不能成毋患有司之不明業患不能
精毋患有司之不公愚生切以爲自誦焉
方今
punctuated:
安，非廉明之吏所宜有也；譽之者亦勿聽。事蹟功罪，斷斷不渝，如齊威所爲烹阿、封卽墨者。斯則名不以疏逖而不章，實不以彌縫而可匿。雖課典之行，裁之自我，而情狀在彼，則旣悉矣。飾名不得以求功，巧文不得以逃罪，尚何吏治之不可飭，而倖位是憂乎？是故考課莫貴乎核名實也。
噫！敎化行，則舉不失人，而吾之明益著；名實核，則法無倖免，而吾之公益彰。明以擇之於先，不才者不得以倖進；公以核之於後，倖進者不得以苟容。賢者進，則庶職脩矣；不肖者不容，則治道粹矣。明主恭己而無爲，大臣布公而弘化，率是道也。故夫師古之意而不泥其法，由今之法而獲古之治，惟公與明者得之。若夫下之自處，則如之何？學患不能成，毋患有司之不明；業患不能精，毋患有司之不公。愚生切以爲自誦焉。方今
translation_en:
…unsettled: this is not a condition that should occur under an incorruptible and discerning official. Nor should those who praise him be heeded. Judgments of accomplishments and failures, merits and offenses, must remain absolutely unwavering, as when King Wei of Qi boiled the administrator of A and enfeoffed the administrator of Jimo. Then a worthy reputation will not remain obscure because its bearer is remote, nor can the truth be concealed by covering up faults. Although the administration of performance evaluations rests on our own judgment, the circumstances of those evaluated will already be fully known. Embellishing one’s reputation will not secure credit, nor will artful documentation enable one to escape punishment. Why, then, should we worry that official administration cannot be put in order, or that men hold office through undeserved good fortune? Thus, in evaluating officials, nothing matters more than checking reputation against reality.
Ah! When moral instruction takes effect, recommendations will not overlook worthy men, and our discernment will become still more evident. When reputation is checked against reality, no one will escape the law by good fortune, and our impartiality will become still more manifest. Through discerning selection at the outset, the untalented cannot gain advancement by chance; through impartial scrutiny afterward, those who have gained advancement by chance cannot merely be tolerated in office. When the worthy advance, the duties of all offices are properly discharged; when the unworthy are not tolerated, the way of government becomes pure. An enlightened ruler maintains a reverent bearing and governs without intervention; his great ministers exercise impartiality and extend moral transformation. All follow this way. Thus, only those who are impartial and discerning can emulate the intent of antiquity without clinging rigidly to its methods, and attain the good government of antiquity through the methods of the present.
As for how those below should conduct themselves, what should they do? In learning, worry about failing to achieve accomplishment; do not worry that the responsible officials lack discernment. In one’s studies, worry about failing to attain mastery; do not worry that the responsible officials lack impartiality. I, an unworthy student, earnestly take these words as an admonition to repeat to myself. At present…

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
聖皇御極名世應會
上懷側席之誠下切拔茅之願耆舊之臣協和
於
朝草莽之士踴躍於野此亦虞廷師師周室
濟濟千載之一時也所以感召而鼓舞之
者徒法云乎徒善云乎愚何幸躬逢其
盛
第四問
黃萼
===
同考試官教諭吳批考究旣詳品藻尤當至論尚
友又得趨向之正一鄉善士非所以限子矣取之
同考試官教諭劉批以鄉之先哲爲問正欲探諸士
願學之志此作獨知所折衷足占素養矣
考試官教授吳批能道其景行之心取之
考試官教授李批敘述詳明評品精確
儒者之學合體用而未始有二致也通顯
晦而未始有二心也夫學術者所以養此
心於未用也然而純駁異其材事功者所
punctuated:
聖皇御極，名世應會。上懷側席之誠，下切拔茅之願。耆舊之臣協和於朝，草莽之士踴躍於野。此亦虞廷師師、周室濟濟，千載之一時也。所以感召而鼓舞之者，徒法云乎？徒善云乎？愚何幸躬逢其盛！

第四問
黃萼

同考試官教諭吳批：考究旣詳，品藻尤當。至論尚友，又得趨向之正。一鄉善士，非所以限子矣。取之。
同考試官教諭劉批：以鄉之先哲爲問，正欲探諸士願學之志。此作獨知所折衷，足占素養矣。
考試官教授吳批：能道其景行之心，取之。
考試官教授李批：敘述詳明，評品精確。

儒者之學，合體用而未始有二致也；通顯晦而未始有二心也。夫學術者，所以養此心於未用也，然而純駁異其材；事功者所
translation_en:
…Our sagely emperor occupies the throne, a figure of epochal distinction answering the needs of the time. Above, he sincerely seeks worthy men, as though leaving part of his seat vacant for them; below, men eagerly wish to advance together, like intertwined couch-grass roots drawn up as one. Venerable ministers work harmoniously at court, while scholars outside official service rejoice in the countryside. This, too, recalls the mutual emulation of the court of Shun and the assembled worthies of the Zhou royal house—a moment encountered once in a thousand years. Can what inspires and rouses them be called mere regulations? Can it be called mere good intentions? How fortunate I am personally to witness such flourishing!

Fourth Question
Huang E 黃萼

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: His investigation is thorough, and his appraisals are especially apt. When he discusses befriending the worthy men of antiquity, he also shows that his aspirations are rightly directed. The designation “a good scholar of one’s own community” cannot set the limits of your attainment. Accept him.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: In asking about the earlier worthies of our province, we intended precisely to explore whom the candidates aspired to emulate. This essay alone shows an understanding of the standards by which to judge them, sufficiently revealing the author’s longstanding cultivation.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: He can express his heartfelt admiration for lofty conduct. Accept him.

Comment by Examiner Li, Professor: The exposition is detailed and clear; the appraisals are discerning and precise.

Confucian learning unites substance and application: these have never had divergent ends. It encompasses both prominence and obscurity: one has never needed a different heart for each. Learning is that by which this heart is nurtured before it is put to use; yet men’s capacities differ in their purity or admixture. Practical achievements are that by which …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
通顯晦而一之者也自是以降學術不明
事功日陋蘇秦張儀公孫衍淳于髡之徒
旣以縱橫遊說之學爲當世所鄙而晏嬰
管仲之功乃孔門所羞稱焉嗣後申韓之
徒主於刑名孫吳之徒主於權術雖足以
爭雄當時而聲施列國固未嘗本於學術
也漢之敝也尚經術而流於訓詁唐之敝
也尚詩賦而流於詞章雖足以闡示幽微
而垂法藝苑固未能施之事功也揆之吾
===
儒體用合一之學益背馳而不可返矣惟
仲舒之三策本於正義明道武侯之事業
本於開誠布公陸贄之告德宗本於尊仁
義黜功利蓋庶幾王佐之材而於學術事
功爲無愧焉下逮於宋豪傑挺生周程之
理學韓范之勳業卓乎不可及矣夷考其
時則吾閩之繼軌而流芳者不無人焉以
理學言之吾道南矣則楊中立見許於穎
昌送歸之日德宇粹然則游定夫器重於
punctuated: 通顯晦而一之者也。自是以降，學術不明，事功日陋。蘇秦、張儀、公孫衍、淳于髡之徒，旣以縱橫遊說之學爲當世所鄙，而晏嬰、管仲之功，乃孔門所羞稱焉。嗣後申韓之徒主於刑名，孫吳之徒主於權術，雖足以爭雄當時，而聲施列國，固未嘗本於學術也。漢之敝也，尚經術而流於訓詁；唐之敝也，尚詩賦而流於詞章。雖足以闡示幽微，而垂法藝苑，固未能施之事功也。揆之吾儒體用合一之學，益背馳而不可返矣。惟仲舒之三策，本於正義明道；武侯之事業，本於開誠布公；陸贄之告德宗，本於尊仁義、黜功利。蓋庶幾王佐之材，而於學術事功爲無愧焉。下逮於宋，豪傑挺生，周程之理學、韓范之勳業，卓乎不可及矣。夷考其時，則吾閩之繼軌而流芳者不無人焉。以理學言之，「吾道南矣」，則楊中立見許於穎昌送歸之日；「德宇粹然」，則游定夫器重於
translation_en:
…that which unites prominence and obscurity as one. From this time onward, learning became obscure, and practical accomplishments grew ever poorer. Men such as Su Qin, Zhang Yi, Gongsun Yan, and Chunyu Kun were already despised by their contemporaries for their learning in diplomatic alliances and itinerant persuasion; even the achievements of Yan Ying and Guan Zhong were considered shameful to mention by the followers of Confucius. Subsequently, the followers of Shen Buhai and Han Fei concentrated on punishments and administrative accountability, while those of Sun Wu and Wu Qi concentrated on strategic expedients. Though these were sufficient to contend for supremacy in their day and spread their fame among the various states, they were never grounded in true learning. The failing of the Han was to esteem classical learning but descend into textual glossing; the failing of the Tang was to esteem poetry and rhapsodies but descend into literary ornament. Though these pursuits sufficed to elucidate obscure subtleties and establish models in the literary world, they could not be applied to practical accomplishments. Measured against our Confucian learning, which unites substance and function, they diverged ever further, beyond recovery.

Only Zhongshu’s three policy essays, grounded in rectifying righteousness and illuminating the Way; the achievements of the Marquis of Wu, grounded in open sincerity and impartiality; and Lu Zhi’s counsel to Emperor Dezong, grounded in honoring benevolence and righteousness and rejecting achievement and profit, approached the capacity to assist a true king. In learning and practical accomplishment alike, these men had nothing to be ashamed of. When the Song arrived, outstanding men arose: the learning of principle of Zhou Dunyi and the Cheng brothers, and the meritorious achievements of Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan, stood unsurpassed. Upon examining that age, we find that our Fujian, too, had men who followed in their footsteps and left a lasting good name. Speaking of the learning of principle, the words “Our Way goes south!” expressed the approval Yang Zhongli received on the day he was sent home from Yingchang; the words “His moral bearing is pure” expressed the esteem in which You Dingfu was held at …

title: 隆慶元年福建鄉試錄
text:
召職學事之初悟理一分殊之㫖造誠中
形外之域均爲得道之深矣凝神靜坐則
李愿中觀氣象於未發之前佩服周旋則
劉彦冲示齋銘於不遠之復契一中之體
守三字之符均爲見道之的矣朱元晦繼
河洛之眞傳本之致知力行以崇實踐之
學蔡季通受四子之遺書發明經世潜虚
以探理數之原禮經屬藁黃直卿詳於民
彝物則之訓矣其何負於吾道之有託邪
===
衍義推明眞景元悉於祈天永命之道矣
其何愧於斯文之自任邪之數子者學術
之醇駁雖未必其盡同然而任秘書者聲
振外夷尉蕭山者練如素任應召而定安
攘之計守郡而致惠政之孚何甞不足於
事功邪其不然者亦其時之未偶耳以事
功言之經理兩河李伯紀抗言於危疑之
日絶貢驕虜曾明仲主議於犯順之秋飭
兵防而國是定抑遼夏而主威張均之有
punctuated:
召職學事之初。悟理一分殊之㫖，造誠中形外之域，均爲得道之深矣。凝神靜坐，則李愿中觀氣象於未發之前；佩服周旋，則劉彦冲示齋銘於不遠之復。契一中之體，守三字之符，均爲見道之的矣。朱元晦繼河洛之眞傳，本之致知力行，以崇實踐之學；蔡季通受四子之遺書，發明經世潜虚，以探理數之原。禮經屬藁，黃直卿詳於民彝物則之訓矣，其何負於吾道之有託邪？衍義推明，眞景元悉於祈天永命之道矣，其何愧於斯文之自任邪？之數子者，學術之醇駁雖未必其盡同，然而任秘書者聲振外夷，尉蕭山者練如素任，應召而定安攘之計，守郡而致惠政之孚，何甞不足於事功邪？其不然者，亦其時之未偶耳。
以事功言之，經理兩河，李伯紀抗言於危疑之日；絶貢驕虜，曾明仲主議於犯順之秋。飭兵防而國是定，抑遼夏而主威張，均之有
translation_en:
…when he was first summoned to take up duties in education. They grasped the purport of the unity of principle and the diversity of its manifestations, and attained the realm in which inner sincerity manifests itself outwardly: both understood the Way profoundly. Concentrating his spirit in quiet sitting, Li Yuanzhong contemplated the disposition of the mind before feelings arose; keeping the teachings close and practicing them in every action, Liu Yanchong presented a studio inscription concerning a return to the Way before straying far. They apprehended the substance of the single Mean and upheld a three-character maxim: both perceived the Way accurately.

Zhu Yuanhui continued the authentic transmission of the He and Luo schools, grounding it in extending knowledge and vigorous practice to exalt learning put into action. Cai Jitong received the writings bequeathed by four masters and elucidated Ordering the World (Jingshi) and Fathoming the Hidden (Qianxu), exploring the origins of principle and number. In drafting the Classic of Rites, Huang Zhiqing treated comprehensively the teachings concerning enduring human relationships and the norms inherent in things. How could he have failed the trust placed in him to preserve our Way? In expounding the Extended Meaning, Zhen Jingyuan fully explained the way to pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate. How could he have been unworthy of his self-assumed responsibility for this cultural tradition?
